   179  with Forced Labor (the ``Report''), regarding the acts, policies, and 
   180  practices of each economy under investigation. For each investigation, 
   181  the Report supports determinations that the acts, policies, and 
   182  practices of each investigated economy related to the failure to impose 
   183  and effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition are 
   184  unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce, and are thus 
   185  actionable under Section 301 of the Trade Act. The Report is 
   186  incorporated by reference into this Notice, and is available on USTR's 
   187  website.
   188  
   189  II. The Acts, Policies, and Practices of the Investigated Economies 
   190  Related to the Failure To Impose and Effectively Enforce a Forced Labor 
   191  Import Prohibition
   192  
   193      Forced labor may be understood as work or service exacted from a 
   194  person under the menace of any penalty for its nonperformance and for 
   195  which the worker does not offer himself voluntarily. There is universal 
   196  international consensus that forced labor is a practice that should not 
   197  be tolerated. Numerous international instruments, such as the United 
   198  Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948); the International 
   199  Labour Organization (ILO) Abolition of Forced Labour Convention, 1957 
   200  (No. 105); the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights 
   201  (1976); and the ILO Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at 
   202  Work and its Follow-up (1998), as amended in 2022, contain provisions 
   203  seeking to eliminate forced labor. Despite this clear and longstanding 
   204  consensus, the use of forced labor across the world continues to 
   205  persist and has even increased in recent years.
   206      The United States has long recognized that eliminating forced labor 
   207  is a moral and economic imperative and that trade is a critical means 
   208  to assist in that goal. For nearly 100 years, the United States has 
   209  prohibited the importation of goods produced with forced labor under 
   210  Section 307 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1307). Commitments to 
   211  prohibit forced labor imports in the United States--Mexico--Canada 
   212  Agreement, as well as in recently signed Agreements on Reciprocal 
   213  Trade, reflect the increasing awareness of this issue and recognition 
   214  that the adverse effects of trade in forced labor goods must be 
   215  addressed.
   216      The existence of forced labor imports in markets across the globe 
   217  has nurtured an economic system that permits the use of forced labor or 
   218  forced labor inputs, penalizing firms and economies that do not. By 
   219  prohibiting forced labor domestically and effectively enforcing its 
   220  forced labor import prohibition, the United States aims to ensure that 
   221  neither domestically produced products nor imports can gain a 
   222  competitive advantage in the U.S. market through the use of forced 
   223  labor. This helps ensure that competition in the U.S. market is based 
   224  on legitimate factors, such as quality and innovation, rather than an 
   225  artificial cost advantage from the illicit use of forced labor.
   226      Economies that fail to impose and effectively enforce a forced 
   227  labor import prohibition fail to ensure that market competition in 
   228  their jurisdiction occurs on a level basis with respect to labor costs. 
   229  While the vast majority of economies prohibit forced labor 
   230  domestically, such measures, if effectively enforced, only discipline 
   231  domestic producers. However, as demonstrated in the Report, these 
   232  measures fail to discipline the influx of imported forced labor goods 
   233  or to prevent domestic producers from using forced labor inputs.
   234  
   235  III. Determinations on Acts, Policies, and Practices Under 
   236  Investigation
   237  
   238      Based on the information obtained during the investigations, as 
   239  reflected in the Report, and considering the advice of the appropriate 
   240  advisory committees and Section 301 Committee, the Trade Representative 
   241  has made the following determinations under sections 301(b) and 304(a) 
   242  of the Trade Act (19 U.S.C. 2411(b) and 2414(a)): the acts, policies, 
   243  and practices of each of the 60 economies covered in the investigations 
   244  are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce, and thus are 
   245  actionable under section 301(b) of the Trade Act.
   246  
   247  [[Page 34274]]
   248  
   249      In particular, the Trade Representative has determined:
   250       The following 54 economies have failed to impose and 
   251  effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced 
   252  with forced labor: Algeria; Angola; Argentina; Australia; the Bahamas; 
   253  Bahrain; Bangladesh; Brazil; Cambodia; Chile; China, People's Republic 
   254  of; Colombia; Costa Rica; Dominican Republic; Egypt; El Salvador; 
   255  Guatemala; Guyana; Honduras; Hong Kong, China; India; Iraq; Israel; 
   256  Japan; Jordan; Kazakhstan; Kuwait; Libya; Malaysia; Morocco; New 
   257  Zealand; Nicaragua; Nigeria; Norway; Oman; Peru; the Philippines; 
   258  Qatar; Russia; Saudi Arabia; Singapore; South Africa; South Korea; Sri 
   259  Lanka; Switzerland; Taiwan; Thailand; Trinidad and Tobago; 
   260  T[uuml]rkiye; United Arab Emirates; United Kingdom; Uruguay; Venezuela; 
   261  and Vietnam.
   262       The following six economies have failed to effectively 
   263  enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced 
   264  labor: Canada; Ecuador; the European Union; Indonesia; Mexico; and 
   265  Pakistan.
   266       Therefore, all of the investigated economies have failed 
   267  both to impose a forced labor import prohibition and to effectively 
   268  enforce such a prohibition.
   269       The failure of each of the investigated economies to 
   270  impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition is 
   271  unreasonable because it: (1) undermines the universal aim of 
   272  eliminating forced labor; (2) permits firms that avail themselves of 
   273  forced labor to produce goods at lower cost and thereby distort market 
   274  conditions for firms that do not use forced labor; (3) undermines the 
   275  profitability of firms that do not use forced labor; and (4) 
   276  contributes to the circumvention of existing forced labor import 
   277  prohibitions.
   278       The failure of each of the above-listed economies to 
   279  impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition 
   280  burdens or restricts U.S. commerce by subjecting U.S. producers to 
   281  unfair competition from forced labor goods both in export markets and 
   282  the U.S. market, and by displacing foreign goods produced without 
   283  forced labor or forced labor inputs into the United States and other 
   284  markets.
   285  
   286  IV. Proposed Actions To Be Taken in the Investigations
   287  
   288      Section 301(b) of the Trade Act provides that upon determining that 
   289  the acts, policies, and practices under investigation are actionable 
   290  and that action is appropriate, the Trade Representative shall take all 
   291  appropriate and feasible action authorized under section 301(c), 
   292  subject to the specific direction, if any, of the President regarding 
   293  such action, and all other appropriate and feasible action within the 
   294  power of the President, that the President may direct the Trade 
   295  Representative to take under section 301(b), to obtain the elimination 
   296  of that act, policy, or practice.
   297      Section 301(c) of the Trade Act authorizes the Trade Representative 
   298  to take certain actions for purposes of carrying out the provisions of 
   299  Section 301(b). Among others, Section 301(c)(1)(B) authorizes the Trade 
   300  Representative to ``impose duties or other import restrictions'' on the 
   301  goods of the foreign country subject to the investigation.
   302      Pursuant to Sections 301(b) and (c), the Trade Representative 
   303  proposes to determine that action is appropriate and that appropriate 
   304  action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices 
   305  would include the imposition of ad valorem duties on all products of 
   306  the 60 economies subject to investigations, except as provided in Annex 
   307  A to this Notice. The proposed exemptions in Annex A include all 
   308  articles and parts currently subject to section 232 tariffs and raw 
   309  materials that if subject to the proposed additional tariffs could lead 
   310  to the unavailability of domestic supply. Annex A also includes 
   311  products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to the 
   312  proposed additional tariffs and certain products that cannot be grown 
   313  or produced in sufficient quantities in the United States or obtained 
   314  from other sources. The proposed exemptions include informational 
   315  materials (e.g., books), donations, and accompanied baggage. Finally, 
   316  the proposed exemptions include articles for which additional tariffs 
   317  may not contribute substantially to the elimination of the investigated 
   318  acts, policies, and practices described above.
   319      For economies that impose a forced labor import prohibition--
   320  Canada, Ecuador, the European Union, Indonesia, Mexico, and Pakistan; 
   321  for economies that have undertaken commitments in their respective 
   322  Agreements on Reciprocal Trade regarding forced labor import 
   323  prohibitions--Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, 
   324  Guatemala, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Taiwan; and economies that have 
   325  imposed a partial regime with the effect of preventing the importation 
   326  of certain forced labor goods--the United Kingdom; the Trade 
   327  Representative proposes additional duties of 10% for products of these 
   328  economies. For all other economies that have failed to impose and 
   329  effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition, the Trade 
   330  Representative proposes 12.5% as the rate of additional duties.
   331      The Trade Representative also proposes a textile mechanism that 
   332  would allow for a certain volume of apparel and textile imports to 
   333  enter the United States at a reduced Section 301 tariff rate. Under 
   334  such a textile mechanism, the volume of reduced-duty imports from 
   335  certain trading partners would be equivalent to the quantity of exports 
   336  of textiles (e.g., U.S. produced man-made and cotton fiber textile 
   337  inputs) from the United States to that trading partner. A certain 
   338  volume of apparel and textile imports would also be allowed to enter 
   339  the United States at the reduced Section 301 rate based on the volume 
   340  of U.S. cotton and cotton products a trading partner imports from the 
   341  United States during a certain period of time.
   342  
   343  V. Response to Significant Comments
   344  
   345      USTR responds below to significant issues raised in the public 
   346  comments and hearings in response to the March 17, 2026, Federal 
   347  Register notice.
   348  
   349  Response to Significant Comments Raising Legal Arguments Regarding 
   350  Findings of ``Unreasonableness''
   351  
   352      Multiple comments raised threshold arguments that the Trade 
   353  Representative should not find that the failure of an economy to impose 
   354  and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods 
   355  produced with forced labor is unreasonable where: (1) an economy has 
   356  domestic laws prohibiting forced labor; (2) where no international 
   357  standards exists which provide an affirmative obligation on economies 
   358  to impose a forced labor import prohibition; or (3) where an economy 
   359  has otherwise made commitments to the United States with respect to 
   360  imposing and/or enforcing a forced labor import prohibition. This 
   361  section takes each of these arguments in turn.
   362      With respect to the first argument, and as explained in the Report 
   363  and above, solely prohibiting forced labor domestically is unreasonable 
   364  because it fails to discipline the influx of forced labor goods or to 
   365  prevent domestic producers from using forced labor inputs. Thus, while 
   366  an economy may have taken steps to ensure that the condition of forced 
   367  labor is extinguished within its borders, the economy nevertheless 
   368  permits market conditions where imported forced labor goods have a 
   369  competitive advantage over U.S. goods imported into their economy.
   370      In response to the second argument, USTR notes the Section 301 
   371  statute,
   372  
   373  [[Page 34275]]
   374  
   375  which governs these investigations, does not require the existence of 
   376  international standards discipling specific conduct as a prerequisite 
   377  to a finding of an unreasonable act, policy, or practice under Section 
   378  301(b) of the Trade Act. As explained in the Report, the definition of 
   379  unreasonable acts, policies, and practices in Section 301(d) 
   380  contemplates circumstances where, as here, acts, policies, and 
   381  practices of a foreign country may not be inconsistent with or violate 
   382  the international legal rights of the United States, but are 
   383  nevertheless unfair. Thus, the statutory structure of Section 301 
   384  contemplates that the Trade Representative may find unreasonable 
   385  conduct on the part of a trading partner even in the absence of 
   386  international standards or obligations.
   387      Third, some comments argued that where an economy has made 
   388  commitments to the United States regarding forced labor import 
   389  prohibitions, including through an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, the 
   390  Trade Representative is without basis to find that same economy's 
   391  failure to impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import 
   392  prohibition is unreasonable. USTR applauds Argentina, Bangladesh, 
   393  Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Indonesia, Malaysia, and 
   394  Taiwan, which have undertaken commitments regarding a forced labor 
   395  import prohibition. However, commitments to take action in the future 
   396  is distinct from forbidding legally the importation of forced labor 
   397  goods, and effectively enforcing such prohibition. Until such time as 
   398  the commitment is implemented, U.S. products will continue to compete 
   399  against forced labor products that have a competitive advantage in

    75  SUMMARY: The United States Trade Representative (Trade Representative) 
    76  has determined under Section 301(b) and Section 304(a) of the Trade Act 
    77  of 1974, as amended (Trade Act), that in each of 60 investigations, 
    78  certain of the acts, policies, and practices of the economy at issue 
    79  are actionable and that action by the United States is appropriate. In 
    80  accordance with the specific direction of the President, the Trade 
    81  Representative is taking actions in each of these investigations by 
    82  imposing tariffs on all products of the investigated economy, with 
    83  certain exemptions as provided in Annexes I and II to this notice 
    84  (Notice). Consistent with the specific direction of the President, for 
    85  an economy that imposes a forced labor import prohibition, has 
    86  committed to impose and enforce such a prohibition through an Agreement 
    87  on Reciprocal Trade (ART), or has imposed a partial regime with the 
    88  effect of preventing the importation of certain forced labor goods, the 
    89  Trade Representative has determined 10 percent is the appropriate rate 
    90  of Section 301 duties, with specific economies subject to a 10 percent 
    91  rate net of a product's most-favored-nation (MFN) duty. For every other 
    92  economy, and in accordance with the specific direction of the 
    93  President, the Trade Representative has determined 12.5 percent is the 
    94  appropriate rate of Section 301 duty, with specific economies subject 
    95  to a 12.5 percent rate net of a product's MFN duty. The Trade 
    96  Representative has also determined, consistent with the specific 
    97  direction of the President, to establish, when feasible, tariff-rate 
    98  quotas (TRQs) for Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, and Malaysia, based 
    99  on each economy's importation of U.S. inputs, to encourage the 
   100  importation by each of these economies of U.S. cotton and textile 
   101  goods, in order to reduce reliance on inputs from other sources that 
   102  are more likely to contain forced labor inputs.
   103  
   104  DATES: The additional rates of duty are applicable with respect to 
   105  products that are entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse 
   106  for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern time on July 24, 2026, 
   107  except that goods loaded onto a vessel at the port of loading and in 
   108  transit on the final mode of transit before 12:01 a.m. eastern time on 
   109  July 24, 2026, and entered for consumption or withdrawn from warehouse 
   110  for consumption before 12:01 a.m. eastern time on July 28, 2026, shall 
   111  not be subject to such additional duty.
   112  
   113  FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: For general questions about this 
   114  Notice, contact Megan Grimball and Philip Butler, Chairs of the Section 
   115  301 Committee, at (202) 395-5725.
   116  
   117  SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
   118  
   119  I. Proceedings in the Investigations
   120  
   121      On March 12, 2026, the Trade Representative initiated 60 
   122  investigations related to the failure of various economies to each 
   123  impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of 
   124  goods produced wholly or in part with forced labor (forced labor import 
   125  prohibition), pursuant to 302(b)(1) of the Trade Act (19 U.S.C. 
   126  2412(b)(1)). See 91 FR 12884 (published March 17, 2026).
   127      On June 2, 2026, the Trade Representative determined that, in each 
   128  of the 60 investigations, certain of the acts, polices, and practices 
   129  of the economy at issue are actionable under sections 301(b) and 304(a) 
   130  of the Trade Act. The Trade Representative also issued a comprehensive 
   131  report, Acts, Policies, and Practices of Various Economies Related to 
   132  the Failure to Impose and Effectively Enforce a Prohibition on the 
   133  Importation of Goods Produced with Forced Labor (Report). Specifically, 
   134  the Trade Representative determined that:
   135       The following 54 economies have failed to impose and 
   136  effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced 
   137  with forced labor: Algeria; Angola; Argentina; Australia; the Bahamas; 
   138  Bahrain; Bangladesh; Brazil; Cambodia; Chile; China, People's Republic 
   139  of; Colombia; Costa Rica; Dominican Republic; Egypt; El Salvador; 
   140  Guatemala; Guyana; Honduras; Hong Kong, China; India; Iraq; Israel; 
   141  Japan; Jordan; Kazakhstan; Kuwait; Libya; Malaysia; Morocco; New 
   142  Zealand; Nicaragua; Nigeria; Norway; Oman; Peru; the Philippines; 
   143  Qatar; Russia; Saudi Arabia; Singapore; South Africa; South Korea; Sri 
   144  Lanka; Switzerland; Taiwan; Thailand; Trinidad and Tobago; 
   145  T[uuml]rkiye; United Arab Emirates; United Kingdom; Uruguay; Venezuela; 
   146  and Vietnam.
   147       The following six economies have failed to effectively 
   148  enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced 
   149  labor: Canada, Ecuador, the European Union, Indonesia, Mexico, and 
   150  Pakistan.
   151       All of the investigated economies have failed to impose a 
   152  forced labor import prohibition and to effectively enforce such a 
   153  prohibition (that is to say, all of the economies have failed to 
   154  satisfy both factors in these investigations).
   155      The Trade Representative proposed to determine that action is 
   156  appropriate in each investigation, and that appropriate action would 
   157  include tariffs on all products of an economy, with certain exemptions. 
   158  The Trade Representative also proposed a textile mechanism that would 
   159  allow for a certain volume of apparel and textile imports from certain 
   160  economies to enter the United States at a reduced Section 301 tariff 
   161  rate. See 91 FR 34272 (published June 5, 2026) (the June 5, 2026 FRN).
   162      The June 5, 2026 FRN invited public comments on the proposed 
   163  actions to be taken in each investigation. The June 5, 2026 FRN 
   164  proposed applying tariffs of 10 percent for each economy that imposes a 
   165  forced labor import prohibition; has taken on commitments related to 
   166  forced labor import prohibitions through an ART; or has imposed a 
   167  partial regime with the effect of preventing the importation of certain 
   168  forced labor goods. The June 5, 2026 FRN proposed applying tariffs of 
   169  12.5 percent for every other economy. The tariff proposals in each 
   170  investigation included exemptions for certain goods, including 
   171  informational materials, donations, accompanied baggage, all articles 
   172  and parts of articles subject to tariffs under Section 232 of the Trade 
   173  Expansion Act of 1962, and certain products identified in Annex A to 
   174  the June 5, 2026 FRN.
   175      As explained in the June 5, 2026 FRN, the proposed exemptions 
   176  included: (a) raw materials that, if subject to the proposed additional 
   177  tariffs, could lead to the unavailability of domestic supply; (b) 
   178  products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to 
   179  additional tariffs; (c) certain products that cannot be grown or 
   180  produced in sufficient quantities in the United States or obtained from 
   181  other sources; and (d) articles for which additional tariffs may not 
   182  contribute substantially to the elimination of the acts, policies, and 
   183  practices determined to be actionable in the investigations.
   184      Interested persons were invited to provide comments regarding the 
   185  scope
   186  
   187  [[Page 47319]]
   188  
   189  of tariff coverage (including the proposed excluded products identified 
   190  in Annex A to the June 5, 2026 FRN and the proposed textile mechanism. 
   191  With respect to the tariff proposals, the June 5, 2026 FRN stated that, 
   192  in considering whether certain articles should be subject to additional 
   193  duties under Section 301 of the Trade Act, USTR will consider the needs 
   194  of the U.S. economy. With respect to comments on the inclusion or 
   195  removal of particular tariff subheadings subject to the proposed 
   196  action, USTR requested that comments address specifically whether the 
   197  products under the tariff subheading are necessary raw materials that 
   198  if subject to the proposed tariff could lead to the unavailability of 
   199  domestic supply; whether additional tariffs would cause serious 
   200  dislocations in the supply of the products and could cause economy-wide 
   201  disruptions, or other similar factors; and whether imposing additional 
   202  tariffs on products under the tariff subheading would be practicable or 
   203  effective in obtaining the elimination of the investigated acts, 
   204  policies, and practices.
   205      USTR also requested public comments regarding the proposed actions, 
   206  including whether the products in Annex A to the June 5, 2026 FRN were 
   207  appropriately excluded; the level of the increase, if any, in the rate 
   208  of duty; whether differential tariff rates should be applied to an 
   209  economy where the economy has made a commitment to the United States to 
   210  impose and enforce a forced labor import prohibition, has imposed a 
   211  forced labor import prohibition, or has imposed a partial regime with 
   212  the effect of preventing the importation of certain forced labor goods; 
   213  and features of the proposed textile mechanism, including the U.S. and 
   214  foreign products to be covered, the relative market opportunities for 
   215  each side, and the tariff rate (if any) to be applied to products 
   216  subject to the mechanism, as well as whether a similar mechanism should 
   217  apply to any other product or sector.
   218      In response to the June 5, 2026 FRN, USTR received over 1,600 
   219  written comments. USTR and the Section 301 Committee held a three-day 
   220  public hearing on July 7, 8, and 9, 2026, regarding the proposed 
   221  actions. During the hearings, over 100 witnesses provided testimony and 
   222  responded to questions. Witnesses included representatives of the 
   223  governments of certain investigated economies, industry associations, 
   224  domestic producers, and non-governmental organizations. The public 
   225  submissions are available at: https://comments.ustr.gov/s/ at docket 
   226  numbers USTR-2026-0265 and USTR-2026-0266. Transcripts of the hearings 
   227  are available on USTR's website.
   228      Following government-to-government consultations pursuant to 
   229  Section 303 of the Trade Act and the publication of proposed actions in 
   230  the June 5, 2026 FRN, additional economies have imposed forced labor 
   231  import prohibitions--Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, 
   232  and Trinidad and Tobago; or undertaken commitments regarding forced 
   233  labor import prohibitions in an ART--Jordan.
   234  
   235  II. Determinations of Action
   236  
   237  A. Overview of Responsive Actions in the Investigations
   238  
   239      On June 2, 2026, the Trade Representative determined that, in each 
   240  of the 60 investigations, certain acts, policies, and practices of the 
   241  economy at issue are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce, 
   242  and are thus actionable under Section 301(b) of the Trade Act. Section 
   243  301(b) provides that upon determining that the acts, policies, and 
   244  practices under investigation are actionable and that action is 
   245  appropriate, the Trade Representative shall take all appropriate and 
   246  feasible action authorized under Section 301(c), subject to the 
   247  specific direction, if any, of the President regarding such action, and 
   248  all other appropriate and feasible action within the power of the 
   249  President that the President may direct the Trade Representative to 
   250  take under Section 301(b), to obtain the elimination of that act, 
   251  policy, or practice. Section 301(b) provides further that actions 
   252  ``within the power of the President'' may include ``[a]ctions . . . 
   253  with respect to trade in any goods or services, or with respect to any 
   254  other area of pertinent relations with the foreign country.''
   255      Section 301(c) of the Trade Act authorizes the Trade Representative 
   256  to take certain, specific actions for purposes of carrying out the 
   257  provisions of Section 301(b). For example, Section 301(c)(1)(B) 
   258  authorizes the Trade Representative to ``impose duties or other import 
   259  restrictions on the goods'' of the foreign country subject to the 
   260  investigation. Section 301(c)(3)(A) provides that actions that the 
   261  Trade Representative is authorized to take may be taken against any 
   262  goods or economic sector on a non-discriminatory basis or solely 
   263  against the foreign country concerned. Section 301(c)(3)(B) empowers 
   264  the Trade Representative to take actions against any goods and economic 
   265  sector ``without regard to whether or not such goods or economic sector 
   266  were involved in the act, policy, or practice that is the subject of 
   267  such action.''
   268      USTR and the Section 301 Committee have carefully reviewed the 
   269  public comments and testimony regarding the proposed actions to be 
   270  taken in each investigation. The Trade Representative informed the 
   271  President of his recommended responsive actions in each investigation, 
   272  including, for each economy, whether to impose 10 or 12.5 percent 
   273  tariffs on all products of that economy or, in the case of specific 
   274  economies, 10 or 12.5 percent tariffs net of a product's MFN duty, with 
   275  exemptions for certain goods. The Trade Representative also informed 
   276  the President of economies that have imposed forced labor import 
   277  prohibitions, or undertaken commitments regarding forced labor import 
   278  prohibitions through an ART, since June 5, 2026. The Trade 
   279  Representative also advised the President that, after considering 
   280  significant comments and testimony on the proposed actions, certain 
   281  products warranted exemption from the tariffs imposed in the 
   282  investigations as they are: (a) raw materials that if subject to these 
   283  tariffs could lead to the unavailability of domestic supply; (b) 
   284  products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to these 
   285  tariffs; (c) products that cannot be grown or produced in sufficient 
   286  quantities or at reasonable prices in the United States or obtained 
   287  from other sources; (d) products for which these tariffs may not be 
   288  effective in obtaining the elimination of the acts, policies, and 
   289  practices of economies found to be actionable in the investigations; or 
   290  (e) certain products of Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El 
   291  Salvador, the European Union, Guatemala, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, 
   292  Switzerland, Taiwan, or the United Kingdom that would encourage these 
   293  economies to fulfill commitments regarding forced labor import 
   294  prohibitions or to encourage these economies to enact and effectively 
   295  enforce a forced labor import prohibition.
   296      On July 23, 2026--after considering and taking account of the 
   297  information and advice provided by the Trade Representative; the 
   298  information, findings, and determinations in the June 5, 2026 FRN; the 
   299  need to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices of

content.text:
Need all specific country determinations through line 1322. Could grep each country names and read around. But for Q6 list Switzerland, Norway, UK, Germany, Taiwan, Türkiye, Japan, Liechtenstein, Hong Kong, India. EU covers Germany; Liechtenstein not investigated likely 12.5? It's not among 60? Wait Liechtenstein not in list of 60. Hmm Q6 asks product of Liechtenstein. Maybe not covered => 0. Hong Kong listed 12.5. Norway 12.5. Switzerland net 12.5. Taiwan net 10. Türkiye 12.5. Japan net 12.5. UK 10. Germany EU net 10. India 10 (newly imposed ban -> 10). Need verify specific determinations. Could use grep. Also Q6(c) changes from proposal: India moved 12.5 to 10 because adopted forced-labor ban; maybe Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago also. Seven economies? Q14 statement 3 says seven economies moved from 12.5 to 10 because each adopted ban. Actual text says additional economies imposed bans: Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago; or Jordan ART. Six bans + Jordan. But three (Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras) were already 10 in proposal due ART commitments. So only India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago moved 12.5→10 due ban. Plus Jordan moved 12.5→10 due ART. That's 4, not seven. The law firm statement says seven moved because each adopted ban — incorrect. Need Q14.

Q6(c): "For which of ten economies in (a) does adopted treatment differ from what was proposed in June 2026, and how? For any economy whose rate itself changed, give reason documents state." Among ten: India changed 12.5→10 due adopting forced labor import prohibition after June 5. UK? Proposal included UK 10 (partial regime); adopted UK 10 same. Taiwan proposal 10, adopted net 10 (cap) changed in structure but rate same? The June proposal said 10% for Taiwan (ART commitments) without net-of-MFN. Adopted gives 10% net of MFN, meaning if MFN below 10 only differential, if above zero. This is a difference in treatment. Japan and Switzerland proposal 12.5, adopted 12.5 net MFN, so differ structurally. Norway proposal 12.5, adopted 12.5 same. Germany/EU proposal 10 (EU imposes forced labor ban), adopted 10 net MFN, structural difference. Liechtenstein not investigated => no duty, different from what? June proposal didn't cover it, so perhaps not "differ" because no proposed treatment. Hong Kong 12.5 same. Türkiye 12.5 same. India changed. Need phrase.

Also Canada 10 adopted; proposal 10 (already had forced labor ban) same. Dominican Republic proposal 12.5 (not on 10 list) adopted 12.5 same. Important Q8 transit.

Need read country determinations for target countries. Use grep patterns around "Switzerland:", etc.

Wait this is within Annex I legal text, headings. Need understand exact HTS structure and country-specific headings. Could be important for Q12 product exemptions. We need know which products are exempt for each economy. Annexes images mostly, but there are readable legal notes that cross-reference specific products/countries. Q12 products: aloe etc, Boswellia, argan oil, sesame seeds for sowing, psyllium husks. They likely appear in Annex II economy-specific exemption lists? The task says annexes not readable, but scenario tells which annex list product is on. Actually Q12 gives subheadings and asks duty; no explicit "on annex list" statement? It gives products and economies. Need determine whether exemption applies based on readable legal text in Annex I/II notes. Some product-specific exclusions are stated in text, e.g. Jordan psyllium and aloe. Q12 likely tests country-specific annex exemptions that are published as images? But task says annexes are images; however some product exemptions may be in readable text? The notes at 2817 onward mention Jordan exceptions. There may be legal text notes for many countries. Need inspect TOC/sections and text around Annex I. We need locate country-specific HTS headings and exemptions. The notice's Annexes images not readable, but the legal text of Annex I (amendments to HTS) is partly readable around lines 2400-2860. It includes headings and product descriptions. Q12 may require reading those.

Let's understand document structure: Annex I begins around line 2350? Search "Annex I".

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

content.text:
Great. Specific product exemptions readable. Q12 asks these products for specific countries. We can determine:
(a) Aloe etc 1302.19.91: Cambodia exempt (country-specific list 9903.06.03); Malaysia? Malaysia's particular articles list only psyllium, Boswellia, argan oil, not aloe. But Malaysia's general image list may include it unknown. Scenario doesn't say on annex. Need use text-only exemption; unless image list. Assumption says product on annex lists the scenario names; Q12 does not name list. Hmm perhaps all these products are in Annex I/II as images, but specific readable text tells. The task says "Annexes are not readable... each scenario below tells you which annex list a product is on." Q12 does not explicitly tell lists, but gives subheading. Perhaps expected to use country-specific specific-article exemptions in readable text. For products not in readable exception, duty applies (unless Annex I general list image, but cannot know). The assumption "product is on the annex lists the scenario names and on no other list published as image" means since Q12 names no list, treat not on any image list. So use readable text only. Thus Malaysia aloe not exempt (not in its particular-article list), so 10%. Cambodia exempt => 0. Good.

(b) Boswellia 1301.90.91: Malaysia exempt; Taiwan exempt; Bangladesh particular list does not include Boswellia (only psyllium and argan), so 10%; Argentina particular list doesn't include Boswellia (psyllium, aloe, argan), so 12.5%. Wait Bangladesh 10% rate; Argentina 10%. Q12(b) asks Malaysia (10% vs exempt => 0), Taiwan (10 net MFN, MFN free => 10% = 10k? but exempt => 0), Bangladesh (10% = 10k), Argentina (10% = 10k). Need check whether Bangladesh/Argentina general Annex I image list includes Boswellia; not readable, and assumption no image list. So taxable.

(c) Argan oil 1515.90.81: Taiwan exempt; Japan? no country-specific particular list for Japan in text; Argan may be in Annex I general list image, but no. Japan net 12.5, MFN 4% => 8.5% = 8500. Indonesia particular list only aloe, not argan => 10% = 10k. Taiwan 0.
(d) Sesame seeds for sowing 1207.40.00: Article-specific exclusion in note (c)(4) applies to all countries! So 0 for Japan, Mexico, Thailand. This is a global exemption, regardless Annex. Good.
(e) Psyllium 1211.90.89: Cambodia exempt => 0; Thailand? no particular exemption; Thailand 12.5%, MFN free => 12.5% = 5000. El Salvador? particular list only aloe, not psyllium, but maybe DR-CAFTA image list; no. El Salvador 10% => 4000. Italy EU net 10; MFN 2% => 8% = 3200.

Need careful: (a) Cambodia 10% but exempt -> 0. Malaysia 10% * 60k = 6k. (b) Malaysia 0; Taiwan 0; Bangladesh 10k; Argentina 10k. (c) Taiwan 0; Japan 8.5k; Indonesia 10k. (d) all 0. (e) Cambodia 0; Thailand 5k; El Salvador 4k; Italy 3.2k.

But need check product "aloe, Tasmanian pepper, coconut and centella" might be a single basket subheading 1302.19.91; yes.

Need read Q9 special rules: 9802, USMCA, 232, Brazil, etc. The note at 2302-2334 covers chapter 98. USMCA Canada/Mexico exemptions. Section 232 exemption in note (f). Q9(f) proposal vs adopted on 232 and informational materials/donations. Need inspect final discussion of comments and annex note. Search "informational materials", "donations", "section 232".

  1531  C. Discussion of Comments on Proposed Product Exemptions
  1532  
  1533      USTR received a variety of comments on the proposed exemption list, 
  1534  including support for the products proposed for exemption and requests 
  1535  to remove certain products from the proposed exemption list. 
  1536  Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1537  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees and in 
  1538  accordance with the specific direction of the President, the Trade 
  1539  Representative has determined to exempt all of the products proposed 
  1540  for exemption in Annex A to the June 5, 2026 FRN, except the non-
  1541  pharmaceutical applications of certain chemical products. Other than 
  1542  the products with non-pharmaceutical applications, as discussed below, 
  1543  the Trade Representative determined not to remove additional products 
  1544  from the exemption list. The Trade Representative determined to exempt 
  1545  certain additional products not included in the proposed exemptions in 
  1546  Annex A to June 5, 2026 FRN.
  1547  1. Support for Keeping Products on the Proposed Exemption List
  1548      USTR received a number of comments expressing support for 
  1549  maintaining certain proposed exemptions. Comments supported the 
  1550  exemption of coffee, mineral tars, certain copper products, iron 
  1551  oxides, coke, aluminum oxide, and coconut products. Other comments 
  1552  expressed support for maintaining the proposed exemptions from Section 
  1553  301 tariffs for products that are subject to Section 232 tariffs. 
  1554  Commenters generally noted that these products are raw materials with 
  1555  limited-to-no availability from domestic sources or cannot be grown or 
  1556  produced in sufficient quantities or at reasonable prices in the United 
  1557  States or obtained from other sources.
  1558      Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1559  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees--and in 
  1560  accordance with the specific direction of the President--the Trade 
  1561  Representative has determined not to remove products other than the 
  1562  non-pharmaceutical applications of certain products from the proposed 
  1563  exemption list, as the remaining products in the proposed exemption 
  1564  list constitute: (1) raw materials that if subject to the proposed 
  1565  additional tariffs could lead to the unavailability of domestic supply; 
  1566  (2) products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to 
  1567  the proposed additional tariffs; (3) products that cannot be grown or 
  1568  produced in sufficient quantities or at reasonable prices in the United 
  1569  States or obtained from other sources; or (4) products for which 
  1570  tariffs may not contribute substantially to the elimination of the 
  1571  acts, policies, and practices found to be actionable.
  1572  2. Determination To Remove Certain Products From the Proposed Exemption 
  1573  List
  1574      Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1575  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees--and in 
  1576  accordance with the specific direction of the President--the Trade 
  1577  Representative has determined to limit the exemption for certain 
  1578  chemicals and chemical products to their pharmaceutical applications. 
  1579  Certain comments noted the health-related applications of products 
  1580  proposed for exemptions and stated that certain ingredients that 
  1581  support U.S. manufacturing of healthcare products are not available in 
  1582  the United States in sufficient quantities to meet domestic demand. 
  1583  Some commenters also requested that these product exemptions be limited 
  1584  to their pharmaceutical applications due to competition with domestic 
  1585  production. Limiting exemptions for these proposed chemical products to 
  1586  their pharmaceutical applications is consistent with the proposal in 
  1587  the June 5, 2026 FRN because an exemption for all applications is 
  1588  broader than necessary to cover goods that have limited availability 
  1589  outside of the investigated economies.
  1590  3. Comments Requesting the Removal of Additional Products From 
  1591  Exemption List
  1592      Some commenters requested that USTR remove other products from the 
  1593  proposed exemption list or otherwise advocated for narrowly tailored 
  1594  exemptions. Industries or products for which commenters expressed
  1595

  1598  opposition to proposed exemptions include beef, avocados, paprika and

  1600  articles containing forgings.
  1601      Commenters suggested, for example, that beef imported from certain

  1603  actionable in these investigations, and that exempting these products

  1662      Having considered the public comments, advice of the Section 301 
  1663  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees, and the

  1665  determined to exempt the following additional products from the scope

  1675  certain antiques, collectibles, and art.
  1676      With respect to certain animal products used as food for animals or 
  1677  an input in such food, commenters noted that these products are 
  1678  incorporated into U.S. animal nutrition programs that support 
  1679  livestock, poultry, aquaculture, and pet food production. According to 
  1680  commenters, there is little opportunity for import substitution for 
  1681  these products and any tariff applied to these products would impose 
  1682  additional costs on U.S. consumers.
  1683      With respect to seeds of a kind used for planting, commenters noted 
  1684  that tariffs on seeds have resulted in increased costs for U.S. seed 
  1685  producers and U.S. farmers. According to comments, tariffs that impact 
  1686  seed movement erode the ability of U.S. seed companies to provide U.S. 
  1687  farmers with pure, high-quality seeds at an affordable price due to the 
  1688  global nature of seed production. Specifically, many U.S. seed 
  1689  companies have foreign operations to take advantage of environmental

  1691  Commenters also noted that the increased costs associated with seed 
  1692  production could reduce choices in the marketplace for consumers as

  1695      With respect to certain vegetable products, commenters noted that 
  1696  certain products falling under the relevant HTSUS subheading are 
  1697  already included in Annex A to the June 5, 2026 FRN, but that the

  1701  production that have no domestic source, including coconut coir, jute

  1706      With respect to in-quota imports of certain sugar and sugar-
  1707  containing products, commenters noted that U.S. sugar producers are

  1712  processing
  1713

  1715  
  1716  facilities rely on certain in-quota sugar to meet U.S. demand and

  1718      With respect to unflavored instant coffee, commenters noted that

  1725  continue to be at a disadvantage producing and innovating ready-to-
  1726  drink and cold brew coffee compared to their foreign competitors if 
  1727  tariffs on unflavored instant coffee are imposed.
  1728      With respect to certain fertilizer inputs and pesticide inputs, 
  1729  commenters noted that imposing additional duties on these chemicals 
  1730  could cause disruptions or shortages in the domestic supply due to the 
  1731  limited availability of certain active ingredients outside of the 
  1732  investigated economies and because these products cannot be produced in 
  1733  the United States in sufficient quantities to meet domestic demand. 
  1734  Commenters also noted that the exemptions would be essential to avoid 
  1735  tariff inversion, causing U.S. manufacturers who produce value-added 
  1736  products to be disadvantaged in comparison to importers of finished 
  1737  agriculture chemical products.
  1738      With respect to certain animal hides and leather products, 
  1739  commenters noted that certain types of exotic leather--including 
  1740  reptile and ostrich--cannot be obtained in the United States because 
  1741  there is no domestic supply. According to commenters, tariffs would 
  1742  cause the migration of exotic leather manufacturing and American jobs 
  1743  to other countries, such as Mexico.
  1744      With respect to certain wood and wood products, commenters noted 
  1745  that certain types of wood and wood product imports--including 
  1746  eucalyptus and certain eucalyptus products--are not available from 
  1747  domestic producers in sufficient quantities to meet U.S. demand. 
  1748  According to commenters, these products are raw material inputs that 
  1749  are used to make timber and crane mats necessary in U.S. construction, 
  1750  powerline installation, and heavy civil infrastructure.
  1751      With respect to vanadium oxides and hydroxides, commenters noted 
  1752  that these products are necessary critical mineral inputs for which 
  1753  there is no or insufficient primary production in the United States and 
  1754  additional tariffs on these materials would cause serious supply 
  1755  dislocations for critical energy-storage infrastructure including AI 
  1756  data centers, electric-grid resiliency, and defense applications. 
  1757  According to comments, vanadium and vanadium electrolytes are necessary 
  1758  inputs across multiple sectors, including steel (including high-
  1759  strength, low-alloy steels for construction, pipelines, and automotive 
  1760  applications); titanium alloys used in aerospace and defense; and 
  1761  critical energy-storage.
  1762      With respect to pig iron, commenters noted that, historically, more 
  1763  than 95 percent of domestic pig iron production has been consumed 
  1764  internally by U.S. integrated steel producers, meaning that iron 
  1765  foundries (like electric arc furnace steel producers) are reliant on 
  1766  imported pig iron. Commenters also noted that other third-country 
  1767  sources of pig iron were limited given that China consumes virtually 
  1768  all of the pig iron it produces, and supply from Russia and Ukraine has 
  1769  been affected by the Russia-Ukraine war. Commenters also stated that 
  1770  pig iron is an essential raw material for iron foundry operations, and 
  1771  that it is melted and mixed with scrap iron and other alloys to produce 
  1772  cast iron. The comments observed that there is no substitute for pig 
  1773  iron, and that additional tariffs on pig iron imports would exacerbate 
  1774  competition they already face from imports of downstream products.
  1775      With respect to certain ferrous products, including pellets, 
  1776  turnings, shavings, chips, fillings, trimmings, and stampings, 
  1777  commenters noted that these products are similar to other products that 
  1778  were proposed to be exempted from tariffs applied pursuant to this 
  1779  action. The comments noted that, like other products already proposed 
  1780  for exemption, iron and steel waste and scrap are important inputs for 
  1781  carbon and alloy steel production, and there is no viable domestic 
  1782  supply for these products.
  1783      With respect to aluminum scrap and waste, commenters noted it is 
  1784  key feedstock material for the U.S. aluminum industry and imposing 
  1785  tariffs would disrupt the supply chains, negatively impacting U.S. 
  1786  aluminum production and, in turn, harming downstream industries and the 
  1787  U.S. economy.
  1788      With respect to aluminum hydroxide, commenters noted that the sole 
  1789  U.S. supplier of aluminum hydroxide is unable to meet U.S. demand and 
  1790  that approximately 40 percent of U.S. supply is sourced from Brazil, 
  1791  with remaining supply supported by producers in Germany and 
  1792  T[uuml]rkiye, among others. According to comments, aluminum hydroxide 
  1793  is an essential, non-substitutable raw material used in critical 
  1794  applications such as sanitation of drinking water, production of flame-
  1795  retardant polymer materials used in defense and industrial 
  1796  applications, production of oil and gas, and refining of aluminum. 
  1797  Companies that use aluminum hydroxide in these and other applications 
  1798  require a stable and cost-effective supply of aluminum hydroxide.
  1799      With respect to ash containing precious metals or precious metal 
  1800  compounds, commenters noted that tariffs on these items would increase 
  1801  costs and disrupt supply chains for products needed to protect U.S. 
  1802  national security, U.S. critical mineral security, and medical device 
  1803  supply chains.
  1804      With respect to certain battery waste and scrap, commenters noted 
  1805  that these products, which are crucial inputs for, among other things, 
  1806  communications and safety technologies, are not available from U.S. 
  1807  manufacturers in sufficient quantities or at commercially reasonable 
  1808  prices. Commenters also noted additional tariffs on these products 
  1809  would result in significant supply chain dislocations by increasing 
  1810  costs, reducing sourcing flexibility, delaying production schedules, 
  1811  and limiting product availability.
  1812      With respect to certain semiconductor manufacturing equipment, 
  1813  commenters noted that these highly specialized tools are not readily 
  1814  substitutable, and that applying Section 301 tariffs to these products 
  1815  would increase investment costs for U.S. manufacturing without 
  1816  materially encouraging the investigated economies to eliminate the 
  1817  acts, policies, and practices determined to be actionable in the 
  1818  investigations. The comments noted that these items are like other 
  1819  products already proposed for exemption.
  1820      With respect to pharmaceuticals and pharmaceutical ingredients, 
  1821  commenters suggested that these products are ingredients that support 
  1822  U.S. manufacturing and cannot be obtained in the United States. 
  1823  Comments further observed that these products were used for health 
  1824  purposes similar to uses for products already proposed for exemption 
  1825  from tariffs.
  1826      With respect to worked shell, commenters noted that there is no 
  1827  U.S. source that can sufficiently meet domestic demand.
  1828      With respect to used worn clothing, and other worn articles, 
  1829  commenters noted that the secondhand apparel market, which is now a 
  1830  mainstream market, has distinct commercial characteristics in 
  1831  comparison to the
  1832  
  1833  [[Page 47333]]
  1834  
  1835  broader retail apparel market, and that the used clothing market is 
  1836  structurally different from new, commercially manufactured clothing. 
  1837  Commenters also noted that additional Section 301 tariffs on used 
  1838  clothing would undermine the goal of eliminating the investigated acts, 
  1839  policies, and practices of the investigated economies; be 
  1840  disproportionate to the value of the goods themselves (i.e., the 
  1841  additional tariffs would be on the resale of the good, not its 
  1842  production); cause serious dislocations in consumer access to 
  1843  affordable clothing; and pose fundamental enforcement challenges in 
  1844  relation to determining the country of origin.
  1845      With respect to certain goods under HTSUS Chapter 97, including, 
  1846  among other things, art, antiques, and collections and collectors' 
  1847  pieces of numismatic interest; goods of zoological, botanical, 
  1848  mineralogical, anatomical interest; extinct or endangered species and 
  1849  parts thereof; and goods of archeological, ethnographic or historical 
  1850  interest, commenters emphasized the unique quality, design, history, 
  1851  sourcing or origin, and supply chains of certain works of art and 
  1852  collectibles, as well as the irreplaceable nature of certain works of 
  1853  art and collectibles. The comments asserted that applying the 
  1854  additional Section 301 tariffs would not be effective in obtaining the 
  1855  elimination of the acts, policies, and practices of the 60 economies 
  1856  determined to be actionable in these investigations and would result in 
  1857  increased costs, administrative burdens, and disproportionate harm to 
  1858  museums, educational institutions, researchers, galleries, auction 
  1859  houses, and micro-, small- or medium-sized enterprises operating within 
  1860  the cultural sector.
  1861      The Trade Representative has determined to add certain animal 
  1862  products; certain seeds; certain vegetable products; certain sugar and 
  1863  sugar containing products; unflavored instant coffee; certain 
  1864  fertilizer inputs and pesticide inputs; certain animal hides and 
  1865  leather; certain wood products; vanadium oxides and hydroxides; pig 
  1866  iron; certain ferrous inputs and waste; certain aluminum scrap and 
  1867  waste; aluminum hydroxide; ash containing precious metals or precious 
  1868  metal compounds; certain battery waste and scrap; certain semiconductor 
  1869  manufacturing equipment; certain pharmaceuticals and pharmaceutical 
  1870  ingredients; worked shell; worn clothing; and certain antiques, 
  1871  collectibles, and art to the list of products exempted from these 
  1872  actions. These products constitute (a) raw materials that if subject to 
  1873  these tariffs could lead to the unavailability of domestic supply; (b) 
  1874  products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to these 
  1875  tariffs; (c) products that cannot be grown or produced in sufficient 
  1876  quantities or at reasonable prices in the United States or obtained 
  1877  from other sources; or (d) articles for which these tariffs may not 
  1878  contribute substantially to the elimination of the acts, policies, and 
  1879  practices of the 60 investigated economies found to be actionable in 
  1880  the investigations.
  1881      The Trade Representative has also determined, consistent with the 
  1882  specific direction of the President, to exempt certain products of 
  1883  Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, the European 
  1884  Union, Guatemala, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, Switzerland, Taiwan, and 
  1885  the United Kingdom from the tariffs imposed on products of that economy 
  1886  in each respective investigation. Exempting these products would be 
  1887  appropriate to encourage each economy to fulfill its commitments 
  1888  regarding forced labor import prohibitions in its ART or, in the case 
  1889  of the European Union, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom, would be 
  1890  appropriate to encourage the economy to impose and effectively enforce 
  1891  a forced labor import prohibition.
  1892  
  1893  E. Determination Not To Exempt Additional Products and Response to 
  1894  Comments
  1895  
  1896      USTR received numerous comments that requested that additional 
  1897  products be added to the exemption list and exempted from tariffs. 
  1898  These comments covered products in a wide range of industries. Most 
  1899  comments that requested that particular products be added to the 
  1900  exemption list based their request on six arguments. These included: 
  1901  (1) requested products have limited or no availability from U.S. 
  1902  source; (2) additional tariffs would increase costs for producers and 
  1903  consumers; (3) tariffs are a competitive disadvantage for U.S. 
  1904  businesses; (4) products requested for exemption are unrelated to the 
  1905  acts, policies, and practices investigated; (5) tariffs would not shift 
  1906  production to the United States; and (6) the tariffs would cause 
  1907  economy-wide disruptions. These six arguments are discussed below, 
  1908  followed by a response to those arguments.

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

    25                  
    26  Actions by the United States in the 
    27                  Investigations Under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 
    28                  1974 of the Acts, Policies, and Practices of 60 
    29                  Economies Related to the Failure of Each Economy To 
    30                  Impose and Effectively Enforce a Prohibition on the 
    31                  Importation of Goods Produced With Forced Labor
    32  
    33                  Memorandum for the United States Trade Representative
    34  
    35                  On March 12, 2026, the United States Trade 
    36                  Representative (Trade Representative) initiated 
    37                  investigations under section 301 of the Trade Act of 
    38                  1974, as amended (19 U.S.C. 2411) (section 301), into 
    39                  the acts, policies, and practices of 60 economies to 
    40                  examine whether any of the economies subject to these 
    41                  investigations fail to prohibit or to effectively 
    42                  enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods 
    43                  produced wholly or in part with forced labor and 
    44                  whether the failure is unreasonable or discriminatory 
    45                  and burdens or restricts U.S. commerce. 91 Fed. Reg. 
    46                  12884 (Initiation of Section 301 Investigations). The 
    47                  economies subject to these investigations are:
    48  
    49                      1. Algeria
    50                      2. Angola
    51                      3. Argentina
    52                      4. Australia
    53                      5. The Bahamas
    54                      6. Bahrain
    55                      7. Bangladesh
    56                      8. Brazil
    57                      9. Cambodia
    58                      10. Canada
    59                      11. Chile
    60                      12. China, People's Republic of
    61                      13. Colombia
    62                      14. Costa Rica
    63                      15. Dominican Republic
    64                      16. Ecuador
    65                      17. Egypt
    66                      18. El Salvador
    67                      19. European Union
    68                      20. Guatemala
    69                      21. Guyana
    70                      22. Honduras
    71                      23. Hong Kong, China
    72                      24. India
    73  
    74  [[Page 47718]]
    75  
    76                      25. Indonesia
    77                      26. Iraq
    78                      27. Israel
    79                      28. Japan
    80                      29. Jordan
    81                      30. Kazakhstan
    82                      31. Kuwait
    83                      32. Libya
    84                      33. Malaysia
    85                      34. Mexico
    86                      35. Morocco
    87                      36. New Zealand
    88                      37. Nicaragua
    89                      38. Nigeria
    90                      39. Norway
    91                      40. Oman
    92                      41. Pakistan
    93                      42. Peru
    94                      43. Philippines
    95                      44. Qatar
    96                      45. Russia
    97                      46. Saudi Arabia
    98                      47. Singapore
    99                      48. South Africa
   100                      49. South Korea
   101                      50. Sri Lanka
   102                      51. Switzerland
   103                      52. Taiwan
   104                      53. Thailand
   105                      54. Trinidad and Tobago
   106                      55. T[uuml]rkiye
   107                      56. United Arab Emirates
   108                      57. United Kingdom
