   110                      59. Venezuela
   111                      60. Vietnam
   112  
   113                  On June 2, 2026, the Trade Representative determined 
   114                  that the acts, policies, and practices of each of these 
   115                  economies are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. 
   116                  commerce and thus are actionable under section 
   117                  301(b)(1) (19 U.S.C. 2411(b)(1)) (Notice of 
   118                  Determinations: 2026-11296; 91 Fed. Reg. 34272) (Notice 
   119                  of Determinations).
   120  
   121                  As a result of these determinations, the Trade 
   122                  Representative proposed to determine in each 
   123                  investigation that action is appropriate under section 
   124                  301 to obtain the elimination of the actionable acts, 
   125                  policies, and practices, including imposing ad valorem 
   126                  tariffs on all goods of each investigated economy, with 
   127                  exemptions for certain goods. To obtain the elimination
   128  
   129  [[Page 47719]]
   130  
   131                  of the actionable acts, policies, and practices in each 
   132                  investigation, the Trade Representative proposed 
   133                  section 301 tariffs. The Trade Representative proposed 
   134                  tariffs of 10 percent ad valorem on goods of economies 
   135                  that: impose a forced labor import prohibition but do 
   136                  not yet effectively enforce it (Canada, Ecuador, the 
   137                  European Union, Indonesia, Mexico, and Pakistan); have 
   138                  undertaken commitments in their respective Agreements 
   139                  on Reciprocal Trade regarding forced labor import 
   140                  prohibitions (Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, 
   141                  El Salvador, Guatemala, Indonesia, Malaysia, and 
   142                  Taiwan); or have imposed a partial regime with the 
   143                  effect of preventing the importation of certain forced 
   144                  labor goods (the United Kingdom). For all other 
   145                  economies whose failure to impose forced labor import 
   146                  prohibitions the Trade Representative has found 
   147                  actionable under section 301, the Trade Representative 
   148                  proposed section 301 tariffs of 12.5 percent ad 
   149                  valorem. In addition, the Trade Representative proposed 
   150                  to establish a textile mechanism that would allow a 
   151                  certain volume of apparel and textile imports to enter 
   152                  the United States at a zero section 301 tariff rate.
   153  
   154                  The Office of the United States Trade Representative 
   155                  (USTR) invited comments by interested persons on these 
   156                  proposed actions and convened public hearings on July 
   157                  7, 8, and 9, 2026. USTR received over 1,600 written 
   158                  comments and testimony from over 100 witnesses at the 
   159                  hearings.
   160  
   161                  The Trade Representative has informed me of the 
   162                  substance of significant comments on the proposed 
   163                  actions in each investigation and provided me his 
   164                  advice on appropriate actions, including tariffs of 
   165                  various rates, exemptions for certain products, and 
   166                  tariff-rate quotas (TRQs) for specific types of 
   167                  products for certain economies. For example, the Trade 
   168                  Representative advised me that after considering the 
   169                  comments and testimony received, certain products 
   170                  warrant exemption from tariffs imposed in connection 
   171                  with an investigation, including because of the needs 
   172                  of the U.S. economy or based on the extent to which 
   173                  imposing tariffs on the products will contribute to the 
   174                  elimination of the acts, policies, and practices of the 
   175                  economies found to be actionable in the investigations 
   176                  described above. These exemptions encompass (a) raw 
   177                  materials that if subject to the proposed additional 
   178                  tariffs could lead to the unavailability of domestic 
   179                  supply; (b) products that could cause economy-wide 
   180                  disruptions if subject to the proposed additional 
   181                  tariffs; (c) products that cannot be grown or produced 
   182                  in sufficient quantities or at reasonable prices in the 
   183                  United States or obtained from other sources; (d) 
   184                  products that if exempted from these tariffs would 
   185                  encourage economies that have made commitments to the 
   186                  United States regarding forced labor import 
   187                  prohibitions to implement those commitments or to enact 
   188                  and effectively enforce a forced labor import 
   189                  prohibition; or (e) articles for which these tariffs 
   190                  may not contribute substantially to the elimination of 
   191                  the acts, policies, and practices of the economies 
   192                  found to be actionable in the investigations described 
   193                  above.
   194  
   195                  The Trade Representative has also advised me that for 
   196                  goods of the European Union, Japan, Korea, Switzerland, 
   197                  or Taiwan, section 301 tariffs that are the net of 
   198                  Most-Favored Nation (MFN) tariffs would be consistent 
   199                  with their respective Agreements on Reciprocal Trade or 
   200                  similar arrangements and would be appropriate to 
   201                  encourage these economies to fulfill commitments 
   202                  regarding forced labor import prohibitions or to enact 
   203                  or effectively enforce such a prohibition.
   204  
   205                  Further, the Trade Representative has advised me that, 
   206                  based on the comments and testimony received, the 
   207                  establishment of TRQs on certain textile and apparel 
   208                  goods is appropriate as a means to encourage the 
   209                  importation by trading partners of U.S. cotton and 
   210                  textile goods, in order to reduce the reliance of such 
   211                  partners on inputs from other sources that are more 
   212                  likely to contain forced labor inputs. Such TRQs, in 
   213                  combination with other tariffs on other products of 
   214                  those trading partners, are appropriate to obtain the 
   215                  elimination of the acts, policies, or practices found 
   216                  actionable under section 301 for those trading 
   217                  partners. The Trade Representative has also
   218  
   219  [[Page 47720]]
   220  
   221                  informed me that establishing these TRQs is not 
   222                  feasible at this time, but that establishing these TRQs 
   223                  will be feasible by September 1, 2026.
   224  
   225                  Finally, the Trade Representative has informed me that 
   226                  following consultation with certain economies in these 
   227                  investigations and publication of the Notice of 
   228                  Determinations, additional economies have imposed 
   229                  forced labor import prohibitions (Cambodia, Guatemala, 
   230                  Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, and Trinidad and Tobago) or 
   231                  undertaken commitments regarding forced labor import 
   232                  prohibitions in an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade 
   233                  (Jordan). As a result of these actions, the Trade 
   234                  Representative has advised me that the goods of these 
   235                  economies should be tariffed at the 10 percent rate to 
   236                  further encourage these economies to effectively 
   237                  enforce such prohibitions, and, in the case of Jordan, 
   238                  to enact and effectively enforce its commitments 
   239                  regarding forced labor import prohibitions.
   240  
   241                  After considering the relevant issues and factors and 
   242                  weighing the relevant considerations, including this 
   243                  information and advice from the Trade Representative; 
   244                  the information, findings, and determinations in USTR's 
   245                  Notice of Determinations; and the need to obtain the 
   246                  elimination of the acts, policies, and practices of the 
   247                  investigated economies found to be actionable under 
   248                  section 301, it is hereby directed as follows:
   249  
   250                  Section 1. Tariffs and Exemptions. (a) Except as 
   251                  otherwise provided in this memorandum, the Trade 
   252                  Representative shall impose the following tariff rates 
   253                  on all goods of the economy for which an act, policy, 
   254                  or practice was found actionable under section 301:
   255  
   256  (i) 10 percent tariff rate: The Trade Representative shall impose a tariff 
   257  of 10 percent on goods of Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Canada, Ecuador, 
   258  El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, 
   259  Mexico, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, the United Kingdom, and Trinidad and Tobago.
   260  
   261  (ii) Tariff rate of 10 percent or 12.5 percent, net of MFN rate: For a 
   262  product of the European Union or Taiwan, where such product's MFN tariff is 
   263  less than 10 percent, the Trade Representative shall impose a section 301 
   264  tariff pursuant to these investigations so that the sum of the MFN tariff 
   265  and the section 301 tariff shall be 10 percent, and where such product's 
   266  MFN tariff is greater than or equal to 10 percent, the Trade Representative 
   267  shall impose a section 301 tariff of zero. For a product of Japan, Korea, 
   268  or Switzerland, where such product's MFN tariff is less than 12.5 percent, 
   269  the Trade Representative shall impose a section 301 tariff pursuant to 
   270  these investigations so that the sum of the MFN tariff and the tariff 
   271  imposed pursuant to these investigations shall be 12.5 percent, and where 
   272  such product's MFN tariff is greater than or equal to 12.5 percent, the 
   273  Trade Representative shall impose a section 301 tariff of zero. Capping 
   274  total duties in this manner is feasible, consistent with the terms of the 
   275  Agreements on Reciprocal Trade or similar arrangements, and appropriate to 
   276  encourage these economies to fulfill commitments regarding forced labor 
   277  import prohibitions or to enact and effectively enforce such a prohibition.
   278  
   279  (iii) 12.5 percent tariff rate: For goods of all other investigated 
   280  economies, the Trade Representative shall impose a tariff rate of 12.5 
   281  percent.
   282  
   283                      (b) The Trade Representative shall exempt from the 
   284                  tariffs imposed as directed in subsection (a) of this 
   285                  section the products identified in the Annex to this 
   286                  memorandum for each economy for which an act, policy, 
   287                  or practice was found actionable under section 301, as 
   288                  the products identified constitute:
   289  
   290  (i) raw materials that if subject to these tariffs could lead to the 
   291  unavailability of domestic supply;
   292  
   293  (ii) products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to these 
   294  tariffs;
   295  
   296  (iii) products that cannot be grown or produced in sufficient quantities in 
   297  the United States or obtained from other sources;
   298  
   299  [[Page 47721]]
   300  
   301  (iv) products for which these tariffs may not be effective in obtaining the 
   302  elimination of the acts, policies, and practices of economies found to be 
   303  actionable in the investigations; or
   304  
   305  (v) certain products of Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El 
   306  Salvador, the European Union, Guatemala, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, 
   307  Switzerland, Taiwan, or the United Kingdom that would encourage these 
   308  economies to fulfill commitments regarding forced labor import prohibitions 
   309  or to encourage these economies to enact and effectively enforce a forced 
   310  labor import prohibition.
   311  
   312                      (c) After considering the relevant issues and 
   313                  factors and weighing the relevant considerations, 
   314                  including potential economic harm and efficacy of 
   315                  tariffs, I determine that the products identified in 
   316                  the Annex to this memorandum shall be exempted from the

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.

Q14 #1: memo says USTR informed TRQs not feasible now but feasible by Sept 1, 2026; section 2 says "as soon as determines feasible," no deadline. So statement "gives USTR until September 1 to set up" is partly correct at best: memo states feasibility expectation, not deadline. Maybe final notice says same. Need distinguish.

Q14 #2: "received over 450 written comments and heard nearly 60 witnesses" — June proposal's proceeding section says over 450 comments and nearly 60 witnesses at April 28-29 hearings. Final notice says over 1,600 comments and over 100 witnesses at July 7-9 hearings. The statement about "the proposed action" maybe referring June proposal? Could be correct if describing initial investigation, but after proposal, comments >1600. Need analyze. Q14 says law firm alert about forced-labor action; statement "USTR received over 450 written comments on the proposed action and heard nearly 60 witnesses." June notice line 109 says over 450 comments "in response to the notice [of initiation]" and hearings April 28-29 nearly 60 witnesses, not the June proposed action. Final says over 1,600 in response to June 5 FRN, over 100 witnesses. So incorrect.

Q14 #3 seven economies moved 12.5 to 10 because each adopted ban. As above, six adopted bans, one Jordan ART; only India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago were 12.5 and adopted ban. Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras already proposed 10 due ART. So incorrect.

Q14 #4 beef and avocados removed from exempt list: final says determined not to remove, so incorrect (they remain exempt). Good.

Q14 #5 every economy whose rate is net of MFN also has own negotiated list of exempt products. Net MFN economies: EU, Taiwan, Japan, Korea, Switzerland. Which have own lists? EU (Part C), Switzerland (D), Taiwan (K), Korea? Specific determination says Korea except Annex I and Annex II Part A only, no country-specific Part? Japan only Part A. So not every. Incorrect. Maybe UK has own list but not net. Good.

Q14 #6 exempted 471 more products, including all sugar and sugar-containing products. Text says additional 471 products, "certain sugar and sugar containing products" — not all. Partly incorrect.

Q14 #7 "no product will bear more than 12.5 percent duty in total." The net-of-MFN caps total at 10 or 12.5 for those; but 232 duties stack (note 52(a) says products subject also to additional duties in subchapter). Also MFN + 12.5 for non-net can exceed 12.5. And section 232 says additional duties apply in addition. So incorrect.

Q14 #8 FTZ privileged foreign status unless eligible domestic status. This matches lines 489-495. Correct.

Q14 #9 court invalid exemption -> goods become subject to duty. This is in memo Sec 4(e) lines 476-483 and maybe final severability. Correct? Need see final section IV. Likely yes.

Q14 #10 of proposal's Annex A, only cutback certain chemicals. Final notice lines 1539-1544 says exempt all proposed except non-pharmaceutical applications of certain chemical products; and "determined not to remove additional products." This statement is correct. But final also added products; "cut back" only chemicals. Yes.

Need Q11 discrepancies. Need find statements in documents that conflict. Potential:
- Dairy exclusion refers to nonexistent Sept 8 dairy scope proclamation.
- Alcohol/Motor scope proclamations say duties apply "in addition to section 232" while original proclamations clause 2 said not apply to 232 articles. Is that a discrepancy or amendment? Q11 asks differences between a statement in one document about what action provides and operative text. Could list.
- Suspension: clause 1 amends "chapeau of Annex II" effective date only, but operative clauses continue Aug 19. Also recital says "temporarily suspended for 3 days" and effective Aug 22; okay.
- September exclusion/proclamation recitals say original duties effective August 19, though suspension changed to Aug 22 and later docs say became effective Aug 22. In alcohol exclusion recital 1 says "effective August 19, 2026" (line 117), then recital 4 says became effective Aug 22. That's internal inconsistency. Similarly all September scope/exclusion docs recite original effective Aug 19. Q11 likely targets these.
- October scope recital 1 says original effective Aug 19, then recital 4 says Aug 22.
- August suspension recitals say effective Aug 19 (historical), okay.
- September scope modification clause 1 says duties apply in addition to 232, contrary to original clause 2. That's operative amendment, not discrepancy? The document doesn't state original had exemption except "except as otherwise provided"; but could be considered change, not inaccurate.
- Q1 asks "Say which kind of event that date and time is measured against in each document." Important: original duty: "goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption" on/after. Suspension: effective date of duties, not event? Clause says effective date shall be 12:01 Aug22. September scope: "goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn..." September exclusion: "goods imported on or after" (not entered), clause2 distinguishes imported before not entered. October scope: entered/withdrawn. Good.

Q2(b) key: original proclamation itself prints Aug 19 in clauses; suspension clause 1 says effective date Aug 22 and amends only chapeau of Annex II, not clauses 1/3. What resolves? Later operative clause 1 of Proclamation 11056 controls as amendment/suspension; plus September docs confirm lapsed Aug22. Could mention specific text still says Aug19 in clauses 1/3, but clause 1 of 11056 sets effective date.

Q2(d) "Did duties need a further presidential action in order to begin? What do later documents say happened in days before they began?" Section 338 says not take effect earlier than 30 days after proclamation. Original proclamation set Aug19 (30 days after July20). Suspension moved to Aug22. Later docs say at 12:01 Aug22 suspension lapsed and duties became effective, and Canada reneged Aug21. No further action needed; lapse automatic. Q2(d) likely wants that.

Need Q1 dates/times for scope exclusions: original three Aug19->Aug22 12:01; suspension Aug22; scope alcohol/motor Sept15; exclusions Sept29; October scope Oct30. Need each doc date signed/published. All 10:
11046 2026-07-20 signed, published 2026-07-23, 91 FR 46639
11047 same 46653
11048 same 46663
11056 signed Aug18, published Aug24, 91 FR 54789
11061 signed Sept8, published Sept14, 91 FR 58311
11062 same 58319
11063 same 58325
11064 same 58331
11065 same 58339
11076 signed Oct23, published Oct30, 91 FR 68861.

Q1 "which documents changed which products are subject to duty" per group:
Alcohol: 11046 original Annex II; 11064 scope mod Part A added, Part B removed effective Sept15; 11061 exclusion Annex removed from importation (ban) effective Sept29, but for goods imported before Sept29 not entered, remain 50% duty; 11056 moved effective date. Perhaps 11061 not "changed products subject to duty" exactly, converts some to import ban.
Dairy: 11047 original Annex II; 11056 moved date; 11062 exclusion Annex ban effective Sept29. No dairy scope modification exists (despite 11062 reference). 
Motor vehicles: 11048 original Annex II; 11065 Sept scope mod Part A added, Part B removed effective Sept15; 11063 exclusion Annex ban effective Sept29; 11076 Oct scope mod Part A removed, Part B added effective Oct30. 
Need note original proclamations exempt section232, later alcohol/motor scope modify to stack. Product groups changed? 11064 and 11065 explicitly say duties apply in addition to 232. Could include under each.

Now Q4 exact dates: Sept10 and Oct1. Need whether September scope modification's "apply in addition to 232" effective Sept15 applies to all products, including Y dairy? No, only Proclamation 11046 alcohol and 11048 motor "as modified in this proclamation." Dairy is 11047 untouched. So Y remains exempt.

But question says "Three Canadian products are each subject to a 25 percent ad valorem duty under section 232 ... Product X listed Annex II alcohol, product Y Annex II dairy, Z Annex II motor. None on any other list." For X and Z, on Sept10 original clause 2 exemption. On Oct1, after scope modification, the 338 duties "shall apply in addition to duties imposed pursuant to section 232." Does the phrase "as modified in this proclamation" mean even products not in Annex I Part A? Yes, it states "The duties imposed pursuant to Proclamation 11046, as modified in this proclamation, shall apply in addition to duties imposed pursuant to section 232." Since X remains subject, 50%. Same Z. Good.

Need section232 duty itself: 25% *100k=25k. Section338 50%*100k=50k. Note 338 base customs value. Total maybe question only asks each. Q4 asks "give the section 232 duty and section 338 duty" not total. We'll show arithmetic.

Q5: Need map product P/Q/R/S to lists and dates. Let's parse.
Original motor Annex II (July 20) subjects products to 50%, effective Aug22. September scope Proclamation 11065 Annex I Part A = newly subject/additional; Part B = no longer subject. Effective Sept15 12:01. October scope 11076 Annex I Part A = no longer subject; Part B = subject. Effective Oct30 12:01.

P: listed Sept Annex I Part A, not original. So P becomes subject Sept15 12:01. At Sep14 3pm: not subject (not original; Sept change not effective). Sep15 12:01: subject (Part A). Oct29 4pm: still subject (unless October Part A/B? P only Sept Part A, not Oct lists per scenario? P not listed Oct. So remains). Oct30 12:01: still subject. Nov3: subject. Note if P is in Sept Part A, did Sept Part A mean "subject" yes.

Q: original Annex II and Sept Part B (removed). Subject from Aug22 until Sept15 12:01; at Sep14 3pm subject; Sep15 12:01 no longer; Oct29 no; Oct30 no; Nov3 no (unless Oct Part B includes Q? no). 

R: original Annex II and Oct Part A (removed). Subject Aug22 through Oct29; at Sep14 3pm and Sep15 12:01 subject; Oct29 4pm subject; Oct30 12:01 removed; Nov3 no.

S: Oct Part B only, not earlier. Not subject Sep14, Sep15, Oct29; becomes subject Oct30 12:01; Nov3 subject.

Need account time: Sept15 12:01 a.m. exactly, so yes. Oct30 12:01 exact.

Q5(b): Oct scope signed Oct23, filed Oct29, published Oct30, applies Oct30 12:01. "Do scope proclamations reach entries made before they apply, and do they provide for refunds?" Need inspect text: Clause 1 says changes effective with respect to goods entered/withdrawn on/after date. No retroactivity/refund provision. The Sept scope likewise. Does any text address pending entries? No. So they do not reach pre-effective entries. Refunds? Silence; no provision. But perhaps language "imported into the United States shall..." without limiting entry? Yet clause effective date controls. Q5(b) answer no, and no refund provision. Could distinguish goods imported before but entered after: effective based on entry, so they do reach entries on/after even if imported earlier. Pre-effective entries unaffected. No refunds stated.

Q5(c): Section 338 waiting period 30 days after proclamation finding. P and S became dutiable Sept15 and Oct30 respectively. P signed Sept8 -> Sept15 is 7 days later. S signed Oct23 -> Oct30 7 days. Do scope proclamations explain how fits waiting period? They recite section 338 30-day limit but don't explain. They rely on original findings/proclamations July20; changes to scope under authority to amend/suspend, not new duty? Need say they do not explain; they simply recite section 338 and original July 20 findings. The 30-day period ran from July20 original proclamation; scope modifications are amendments, effective 7 days after signing. Whether that satisfies statute is not addressed. Q5(c) asks "As these documents describe section 338, there is a waiting period before additional duties may take effect. How long after signing did P and S become dutiable, and do the scope proclamations explain how that fits the waiting period?" Answer: P 7 days, S 7 days; no explanation beyond recitals; perhaps because not new duties but modifications to existing duties whose 30 days ran from July20. We should flag.

Q6 calculations. Need section301 rates and base. Use values $100k, MFN 4%.
(1) Switzerland: net 12.5; MFN 4 <12.5 => 301 8.5% = $8,500; total MFN 4,000 + 8,500 = 12,500.
(2) Norway: 12.5% = 12,500; total 16,500.
(3) UK: 10% = 10,000; total 14,000.

    65                  Proclamation 11012 of February 20, 2026
    66  
    67                  
    68  Imposing a Temporary Import Surcharge To Address 
    69                  Fundamental International Payments Problems
    70  
    71                  By the President of the United States of America
    72  
    73                  A Proclamation
    74  
    75                  1. The United States plays a pivotal role in shaping 
    76                  the global economy. At the same time, the United States 
    77                  faces various threats to its own economy and national 
    78                  interests. Sometimes, the United States faces 
    79                  fundamental international payments problems, such as 
    80                  large and serious balance-of-payments deficits, an 
    81                  imminent and significant depreciation of its currency 
    82                  in foreign exchange markets, or an international 
    83                  balance-of-payments disequilibrium. These problems can, 
    84                  among other things, endanger the ability of the United 
    85                  States to finance its spending, erode investor 
    86                  confidence in the economy, and distress the financial 
    87                  markets.
    88  
    89                  2. Special import measures to restrict imports, such as 
    90                  surcharges and quotas, are key tools to protect the 
    91                  economy and national security of the United States, 
    92                  and, in certain circumstances, they are required to 
    93                  deal with fundamental international payments problems.
    94  
    95                  3. Given the gravity of fundamental international 
    96                  payments problems and the importance of import 
    97                  restrictions as economic, national security, and 
    98                  foreign policy tools, Federal law, including section 
    99                  122 of the Trade Act of 1974 (19 U.S.C. 2132) (section 
   100                  122), empowers the President to take action through 
   101                  surcharges and other special import restrictions to 
   102                  address fundamental international payments problems.
   103  
   104                  4. I have received certain requested information and 
   105                  opinions from senior officials on whether any 
   106                  fundamental international payments problems exist and 
   107                  the extent to which such problems could impair United 
   108                  States national interests, including economic and 
   109                  national security interests. The information and 
   110                  opinions discuss, among other things, the state of the 
   111                  balance of payments of the United States, the standing 
   112                  of the United States dollar in foreign exchange 
   113                  markets, and the state of international balances of 
   114                  payments. I have also received opinions and 
   115                  recommendations from senior officials on whether 
   116                  special import measures to restrict imports are 
   117                  required to address any fundamental international 
   118                  payments problems. These opinions address, among other 
   119                  things, whether a surcharge in the form of ad valorem 
   120                  duties is required to restrict imports to deal with 
   121                  large and serious United States balance-of-payments 
   122                  deficits, to prevent an imminent and significant 
   123                  depreciation of the United States dollar in foreign 
   124                  exchange markets, or to cooperate with other countries 
   125                  in correcting an international balance-of-payments 
   126                  disequilibrium.
   127  
   128                  5. These senior officials have informed me that 
   129                  fundamental international payments problems within the 
   130                  meaning of section 122 exist and that special import 
   131                  measures to restrict imports are required to address 
   132                  these problems. Specifically, my advisors have 
   133                  determined that an import surcharge in the form of ad 
   134                  valorem duties is required to deal with large and 
   135                  serious United States balance-of-payments deficits. My 
   136                  advisors have also opined that certain products should 
   137                  not be subject to the surcharge because of the needs of 
   138                  the United States economy and that the recommended 
   139                  exceptions are consistent with the limitations of 
   140                  section 122, the purposes of section 122, and the 
   141                  national interest of the United States.
   142  
   143  [[Page 9340]]
   144  
   145                  6. Among other things, I have been informed by my 
   146                  advisors that the United States balance-of-payments 
   147                  position, under any reasonable understanding of the 
   148                  term in the context of section 122, is currently a 
   149                  large and serious deficit. My advisors have studied 
   150                  different methods of evaluating balance-of-payments 
   151                  deficits, including calculations based on current-
   152                  account statistics. In my advisors' opinions, under any 
   153                  of these methods, the United States balance-of-payments 
   154                  position is a large and serious deficit.
   155  
   156                  7. For instance, my advisors have informed me that the 
   157                  United States runs a deficit in selling goods and 
   158                  services overseas, as reported by the United States 
   159                  Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) in the ``balance on 
   160                  goods and services''; has recently reflected quarterly 
   161                  deficits in its return on investment or labor, as 
   162                  reported by the BEA in the ``balance on primary 
   163                  income''; and runs a deficit in voluntary transfers, 
   164                  such as remittances, as reported by the BEA in the 
   165                  ``balance on secondary income.'' In other words, the 
   166                  United States runs a trade deficit, does not currently 
   167                  make a net income from the capital and labor that it 
   168                  deploys abroad, and experiences more transfer payments, 
   169                  on net, flowing out of the country than into the 
   170                  country.
   171  
   172                  8. As my advisors have informed me, the United States 
   173                  runs a substantial trade deficit. The large, 
   174                  persistent, and serious annual United States goods 
   175                  trade deficit has grown by over 40 percent in the past 
   176                  5 years alone, reaching $1.2 trillion in 2024. In 2025, 
   177                  the United States goods trade deficit remained at 
   178                  approximately $1.2 trillion. The effects of this 
   179                  deficit are serious, and this deficit contributes to 
   180                  the fundamental international payments problems facing 
   181                  the United States.
   182  
   183                  9. As my advisors have also informed me, the annual 
   184                  balance on the United States primary income turned 
   185                  negative for the first time since at least 1960 in 
   186                  2024. From 1960 to 2023, the United States ran a 
   187                  surplus in its annual balance on primary income. That 
   188                  positive balance on primary income served as a 
   189                  stabilizing force for the United States balance-of-
   190                  payments position even in the face of large and 
   191                  persistent trade deficits. In 2024, however, the 
   192                  balance on primary income turned negative and thus 
   193                  ceased to serve as a counterweight to the trade deficit 
   194                  in the United States current account. Indeed, in 2024, 
   195                  the United States maintained a current account deficit 
   196                  of 4.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), almost 
   197                  double the current account deficit of approximately 2.0 
   198                  percent that prevailed between 2013 and 2019, and 
   199                  larger than that which prevailed from 2019 to 2023. As 
   200                  a share of GDP, the staggering deficit of 4.0 percent 
   201                  represented the biggest annual current account deficit 
   202                  since 2008.
   203  
   204                  10. As my advisors have also informed me, the net 
   205                  international-investment position of the United States 
   206                  is in an ongoing decline. According to the BEA, at the 
   207                  end of 2024, the net international-investment position 
   208                  of the United States, as a share of GDP, was negative 
   209                  90 percent, a sharp deterioration from the average of 
   210                  negative 41 percent in the decade between 2010 and 
   211                  2020. In my advisors' view, this is a highly atypical 
   212                  position for a country, particularly the United States. 
   213                  Indeed, both in terms of United States dollars and as a 
   214                  share of GDP, this represents one of the most negative 
   215                  net international-investment positions of any developed 
   216                  country. Because the current account is one of the 
   217                  primary drivers of changes in the net international-
   218                  investment position, the atypically large negative net 
   219                  international-investment position of the United States 
   220                  shows that the United States balance-of-payments 
   221                  deficit is large and serious.
   222  
   223                  11. Further, as my advisors have informed me, the 
   224                  balance on secondary income of the United States has 
   225                  been persistently in a deficit since the 1960s.
   226  
   227                  12. According to my advisors, an import surcharge in 
   228                  the form of ad valorem duties is required to address 
   229                  these fundamental international payments problems. In 
   230                  my advisors' opinions, imposing an import surcharge 
   231                  would deal with the large and serious United States 
   232                  balance-of-payments deficit. My advisors have further 
   233                  recommended that certain products should not be subject 
   234                  to the surcharge because of the needs of the United 
   235                  States economy
   236  
   237  [[Page 9341]]
   238  
   239                  and have opined that a surcharge with certain 
   240                  exceptions would more effectively deal with the 
   241                  balance-of-payments deficit than would a surcharge 
   242                  without the exceptions.
   243  
   244                  13. After considering the information, opinions, and 
   245                  recommendations that have been provided to me by senior 
   246                  officials, among other relevant information and 
   247                  considerations, I find that fundamental international 
   248                  payments problems within the meaning of section 122 
   249                  exist; that those problems significantly harm United 
   250                  States national interests, including economic and 
   251                  national security interests; and that special measures 
   252                  to restrict imports are required to address those 
   253                  problems, as authorized by section 122. Specifically, I 
   254                  find that a surcharge in the form of ad valorem duties 
   255                  on certain imports is required to deal with the United 
   256                  States' large and serious balance-of-payments deficit. 
   257                  Accordingly, I impose, for a period of 150 days, a 
   258                  temporary import surcharge of 10 percent ad valorem, as 
   259                  described below, on articles imported into the United 
   260                  States, effective February 24, 2026.
   261  
   262                  14. Because of the needs of the United States economy, 
   263                  I determine that the surcharge imposed in this 
   264                  proclamation shall not apply to the following products, 
   265                  as further detailed in Annexes I and II to this 
   266                  proclamation:
   267  
   268                  (a) certain critical minerals;
   269  
   270                  (b) metals used in currency and bullion;
   271  
   272                  (c) energy and energy products;
   273  
   274                  (d) natural resources and fertilizers that cannot be 
   275                  grown, mined, or otherwise produced in the United 
   276                  States or grown, mined, or otherwise produced in 
   277                  sufficient quantities to meet domestic demand;
   278  
   279                  (e) certain agricultural products, including beef, 
   280                  tomatoes, and oranges;
   281  
   282                  (f) pharmaceuticals and pharmaceutical ingredients;
   283  
   284                  (g) certain electronics;
   285  
   286                  (h) passenger vehicles, certain light trucks, certain 
   287                  medium- and heavy-duty vehicles, buses, and certain 
   288                  parts of passenger vehicles, light trucks, medium- and 
   289                  heavy-duty vehicles, and buses;
   290  
   291                  (i) certain aerospace products;
   292  
   293                  (j) information materials, donations, and accompanied 
   294                  baggage;
   295  
   296                  (k) all articles and parts of articles currently or 
   297                  that later become subject to additional import 
   298                  restrictions imposed pursuant to section 232 of the 
   299                  Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as amended (19 U.S.C. 
   300                  1862) (section 232);

content.text: Surcharge 150 days from Feb24 ends ~July24 2026. So by September no. But is there extension/termination? 150 days enough. Need exact end date arithmetic: Feb24 +150 days. Feb 24 to Aug? Let's calculate. Feb 24 + 150 days: Feb remaining 4 days (to Feb28?) 2026 not leap. Day 0 Feb24. Add 150 = July24? Feb 24->Mar24 28 days, ->Apr24 31 (59), ->May24 30 (89), ->Jun24 31 (120), ->Jul24 30 (150). So expires July24, 2026. Effective Feb24. Q10(f) Sept no surcharge. It may have been superseded? Search later "surcharge" 2026.

content.text:
No extension. So Q10(f): IEEPA ended by EO 14389 Feb20 (collection as soon as practicable); 10% surcharge expired after 150 days around July24. Neither applies Sep.

But Q15 includes entries across dates, need IEEPA and surcharge applicable on those dates. We must research all additional duties on Canadian aluminum extrusions over time. This is complex. Need identify:
- IEEPA northern border duties from Feb 2025, with amendments, exemptions, increases.
- Section 232 aluminum duties 25%? 50%? Dates.
- Section 338 50% from Aug22 2026.
- Section 301 10% Canada from July24 2026, but section232 articles exempt.
- Temporary import surcharge 10% Feb24-Jul24 2026, but section232 articles exempt.
- Any other additional duties: perhaps "Canada reciprocal" IEEPA, "fentanyl" etc. Q15 says every additional duty Federal Register imposed on these goods on entry date counts. Need list and explain why not owed for each other additional duty then in force. Could include:
  - IEEPA northern border 25% (Feb 4, 2025? effective Feb4, then paused, then March4).
  - IEEPA reciprocal tariffs 10%? Canada except USMCA.
  - Section 232 aluminum 25% (March 12, 2025) then 50% (June 4, 2025?) maybe.
  - Section 232 steel/aluminum derivative 25%? 
  - Section 338 motor vehicle 50% from Aug22 2026.
  - Section 301 forced labor 10% from July24 2026 but 232 exempt.
  - Temporary import surcharge 10% Feb24-Jul24 2026, but 232 exempt.
  - Maybe "10% baseline reciprocal tariff" ended by EO 14389 Feb20 2026.
  - IEEPA Canada northern border ended Feb20 2026.
Need know exact duty rates and scope dates across 2025-2026. Q15 entry dates chosen to test: Feb10 2025, Mar6, Mar10, Mar14, Jun3, Jun10, Aug5 2025, Mar2 2026, Jun10 2026, Jul27 2026, Aug25 2026, Sep14, Sep16, Nov10 2026.

Let's research IEEPA northern border chronology. Read EO 14193, EO 14197, amendments, and later. Use search results. Start metadata maybe enough.

    42                  I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of 
    43                  America, find that the sustained influx of illicit 
    44                  opioids and other drugs has profound consequences on 
    45                  our Nation, endangering lives and putting a severe 
    46                  strain on our healthcare system, public services, and

    49                  This challenge threatens the fabric of our society.

    53                  in these challenges, including by failing to devote 
    54                  sufficient attention and resources or meaningfully 
    55                  coordinate with United States law enforcement partners 
    56                  to effectively stem the tide of illicit drugs.
    57  
    58                  Drug trafficking organizations (DTOs) are the world's 
    59                  leading producers of fentanyl, methamphetamine, 
    60                  cocaine, and other illicit drugs, and they cultivate, 
    61                  process, and distribute massive quantities of narcotics 
    62                  that fuel addiction and violence in communities across 
    63                  the United States. These DTOs often collaborate with 
    64                  transnational cartels to smuggle illicit drugs into the 
    65                  United States, utilizing clandestine airstrips, 
    66                  maritime routes, and overland corridors.
    67  
    68                  The challenges at our southern border are foremost in 
    69                  the public consciousness, but our northern border is 
    70                  not exempt from these issues. Criminal networks are 
    71                  implicated in human trafficking and smuggling 
    72                  operations, enabling unvetted illegal migration across 
    73                  our northern border. There is also a growing presence 
    74                  of Mexican cartels operating fentanyl and nitazene 
    75                  synthesis labs in Canada. The flow of illicit drugs 
    76                  like fentanyl to the United States through both illicit 
    77                  distribution networks and international mail--due, in 
    78                  the case of the latter, to the existing administrative 
    79                  exemption from duty and taxes, also known as de 
    80                  minimis, under section 1321 of title 19, United States 
    81                  Code--has created a public health crisis in the United 
    82                  States, as outlined in the Presidential Memorandum of 
    83                  January 20, 2025 (America First Trade Policy) and 
    84                  Executive Order 14157 of January 20, 2025 (Designating 
    85                  Cartels and Other Organizations as Foreign Terrorist 
    86                  Organizations and Specially Designated Global 
    87                  Terrorists). With respect to smuggling of illicit drugs 
    88                  across our northern border, Canada's Financial 
    89                  Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre recently 
    90                  published a study on the laundering of proceeds of 
    91                  illicit synthetic opioids, which recognized Canada's 
    92                  heightened domestic production of fentanyl, largely 
    93                  from British Columbia, and its growing footprint within 
    94                  international narcotics distribution. Despite a North 
    95                  American dialogue on the public health impacts of 
    96                  illicit drugs since 2016, Canadian officials have 
    97                  acknowledged that the problem has only grown. And while 
    98                  U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) within the 
    99                  Department of Homeland Security seized, comparatively, 
   100                  much less fentanyl from Canada than from Mexico last 
   101                  year, fentanyl is so potent that even a very small 
   102                  parcel of the drug can cause many deaths and

   106                  destruction to America families. In fact, the amount of 
   107                  fentanyl that crossed the northern border last year

   110                  Immediate action is required to finally end this public 
   111                  health crisis and national emergency, which will not 
   112                  happen unless the compliance and cooperation of Canada 
   113                  is assured.

   115                  I hereby determine and order:

   117                  Section 1. (a) As President of the United States, my 
   118                  highest duty is the defense of the country and its 
   119                  citizens. A Nation without borders is not a nation at 
   120                  all. I will not stand by and allow our sovereignty to 
   121                  be eroded, our laws to be trampled, our citizens to be 
   122                  endangered, or our borders to be disrespected anymore.
   123  
   124                  I previously declared a national emergency with respect

   126                  influx of illegal aliens and illicit drugs into the 
   127                  United States in Proclamation 10886 of January 20, 2025 
   128                  (Declaring a National Emergency at the Southern 
   129                  Border). Pursuant to the NEA, I hereby expand the scope

   132                  Americans, including the public health crisis of deaths 
   133                  due to the use of fentanyl and other illicit drugs, and 
   134                  the failure of Canada to do more to arrest, seize, 
   135                  detain, or otherwise intercept DTOs, other drug and 
   136                  human traffickers, criminals at large, and drugs. In 
   137                  addition, this failure to act on the part of Canada 
   138                  constitutes an unusual and extraordinary threat, which 
   139                  has its source in substantial part outside the United 
   140                  States, to the national security and foreign policy of 
   141                  the United States. I hereby declare and reiterate a 
   142                  national emergency under the NEA and IEEPA to deal with 
   143                  that threat. This national emergency requires decisive 
   144                  and immediate action, and I have decided to impose, 
   145                  consistent with law, ad valorem tariffs on articles 
   146                  that are products of Canada set forth in this order. In 
   147                  doing so, I invoke my authority under section 
   148                  1702(a)(1)(B) of IEEPA, and specifically find that 
   149                  action under other authority to impose tariffs is 
   150                  inadequate to address this unusual and extraordinary 
   151                  threat.
   152

   154                  defined by the Federal Register notice described in

   159                  valorem rate of duty. Such rate of duty shall apply

   192                      (c) The rates of duty established by this order are 
   193                  in addition to any other duties, fees, exactions, or 
   194                  charges applicable to such imported articles.

Key: USMCA goods exempt from IEEPA beginning Mar7. Prior Mar4-6 they weren't exempt? EO 14193 didn't exempt USMCA. So entries Mar6 no USMCA exemption (if qualified), duty 25%. Mar10/14 USMCA exempt. Non-USMCA 25%.

Then July31 2025 amendment (EO 14325) likely increases to 35%? Let's read.

    80                  found and advised me of the Secretary's opinion that 
    81                  aluminum is being imported into the United States in 
    82                  such quantities and under such circumstances as to 
    83                  threaten to impair the national security of the United 
    84                  States.
    85  
    86                  2. In Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    87                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), I 
    88                  concurred in the Secretary's finding that aluminum was 
    89                  being imported into the United States in such 
    90                  quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten 
    91                  to impair the national security of the United States, 
    92                  and decided to adjust the imports of aluminum articles 
    93                  by imposing a 10 percent ad valorem tariff on such 
    94                  articles imported from most countries. Proclamation 
    95                  9704 further stated that any country with which the 
    96                  United States has a security relationship is welcome to 
    97                  discuss alternative ways to address the threatened 
    98                  impairment of the national security caused by imports 
    99                  from that country, and noted that, should the United 
   100                  States and any such country arrive at a satisfactory 
   101                  alternative means to address the threat to the national 
   102                  security such that I determine that imports from that 
   103                  country no longer threaten to impair the national 
   104                  security, I may remove or modify the restriction on 
   105                  aluminum articles imports from that country and, if 
   106                  necessary, adjust the tariff as it applies to other 
   107                  countries, as the national security interests of the 
   108                  United States require.
   109  
   110                  3. In Proclamation 9704, I also directed the Secretary 
   111                  to monitor imports of aluminum articles and inform me 
   112                  of any circumstances that in the Secretary's opinion 
   113                  might indicate the need for further action under 
   114                  section 232 with respect to such imports. Pursuant to 
   115                  Proclamation 9704, the Secretary was authorized to 
   116                  provide relief from the additional duties, based on a 
   117                  request from a directly affected party located in the 
   118                  United States, for any aluminum article determined not 
   119                  to be produced in the United States in a sufficient and 
   120                  reasonably available amount or of a satisfactory

   122                  considerations. Proclamation 9776 of August 29, 2018,

   124                  authorized the Secretary to provide relief from certain 
   125                  tariffs on other aluminum products and derivatives set 
   126                  forth in those proclamations.
   127  
   128                  4. In subsequent proclamations, the President adjusted 
   129                  the tariffs applicable to aluminum articles imports 
   130                  from Argentina, Australia, Canada, Mexico, the European 
   131                  Union (EU), and the United Kingdom (UK), after engaging 
   132                  in discussions with each of those parties on 
   133                  alternative ways to address the threat to the national 
   134                  security from such imports.

   137                  the 10 percent ad valorem tariff imposed by 
   138                  Proclamation 9704 that mitigated the threatened 
   139                  impairment of our national security, aluminum imports 
   140                  into the United States have continued at unacceptable 
   141                  levels as the global aluminum excess capacity crisis 
   142                  continues. In addition, the exclusion of certain 
   143                  countries

   147                  and products from the tariff and efforts by foreign 
   148                  producers to circumvent the tariff have undermined the 
   149                  purpose of Proclamation 9704, which was to adjust the 
   150                  level of imports of aluminum to remove the threatened 
   151                  impairment of the national security. This has again 
   152                  resulted in aluminum smelter capacity utilization rates 
   153                  in the domestic aluminum industry that are well below 
   154                  the target level recommended in the Secretary's January

   156                  tariff of 10 percent ad valorem is not high enough to 
   157                  address the threatened impairment to our national

   182                  additional adjustments to section 232 tariffs on 
   183                  aluminum need to be made, including limiting exemptions 
   184                  and increasing the tariff rate.

    91                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), 
    92                  Proclamation 10896 of February 10, 2025 (Adjusting 
    93                  Imports of Steel Into the United States), and 
    94                  Proclamation 10947 of June 3, 2025 (Adjusting Imports 
    95                  of Aluminum and Steel Into the United States), which 
    96                  increased the additional ad valorem rate of duty and 
    97                  eliminated loopholes and exemptions in the
    98  
    99  [[Page 18202]]
   100  
   101                  aluminum and steel tariff regimes. For example, under 
   102                  the aluminum and steel tariff regimes, domestic 
   103                  capacity utilization has increased from approximately 
   104                  39 percent in 2017 to approximately 50.4 percent at 
   105                  present for aluminum production and from approximately 
   106                  72.3 percent in 2017 to approximately 77.2 percent at 
   107                  present for steel production, which is closer to the 
   108                  Secretary's recommended objective of achieving a 
   109                  sustained domestic capacity utilization of 80 percent 
   110                  for aluminum and steel production. In the Secretary's 
   111                  opinion, the domestic capacity utilization for aluminum 
   112                  and steel production would not be as high as it is if 
   113                  not for the aluminum and steel tariff regimes imposed 
   114                  under section 232.
   115  
   116                  5. Based on his monitoring of imports of metal 
   117                  products, the Secretary informed me that there are 
   118                  opportunities to continue to improve the operation of 
   119                  the tariff regimes to address more effectively the 
   120                  national security threats found in Proclamation 9704, 
   121                  Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 10962. For example, 
   122                  the Secretary recommended that I clarify that ad 
   123                  valorem tariffs apply to the full customs value of 
   124                  metal articles, and he recommended that the tariffs 
   125                  apply to the full customs value of derivative products.
   126  
   127                  6. The Secretary further recommended that I modify the 
   128                  scope of derivative articles that are subject to the 
   129                  tariffs imposed under Proclamation 9704 and 
   130                  Proclamation 9705. In the Secretary's view, certain 
   131                  derivative articles should remain subject to the 
   132                  tariffs imposed under Proclamation 9704, as amended, 
   133                  and Proclamation 9705, as amended, to prevent 
   134                  circumvention of the tariffs on aluminum or steel 
   135                  articles or because the derivative article sufficiently 
   136                  contributes to the applicable national security threat 
   137                  found in Proclamation 9704 and Proclamation 9705. By 
   138                  contrast, in the Secretary's view, other derivative 
   139                  articles should no longer be subject to the tariffs 
   140                  imposed under Proclamation 9704 and Proclamation 9705 
   141                  because continuing the tariffs does not at this time 
   142                  make a significant contribution to effectively 
   143                  addressing the identified national security threats.
   144  
   145                  7. After considering the current information, opinions, 
   146                  and recommendations newly provided by the Secretary; 
   147                  the factors in section 232 (19 U.S.C. 1862(d)); the 
   148                  need to address the national security threats found in 
   149                  Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 
   150                  10962; and other relevant factors and information, I 
   151                  determine that it is necessary and appropriate to 
   152                  modify, as further described below, the tariff regimes 
   153                  for metal products imposed in Proclamation 9704, as 
   154                  amended; Proclamation 9705, as amended; and 
   155                  Proclamation 10962.
   156  
   157                  8. I determine that it is necessary and appropriate to 
   158                  modify the tariffs imposed pursuant to Proclamation 
   159                  9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as amended; and 
   160                  Proclamation 10962 so that they apply to the full 
   161                  customs value of aluminum, steel, and copper articles 
   162                  and their derivatives, regardless of metal content.
   163  
   164                  9. The full-value ad valorem tariffs on aluminum and 
   165                  steel articles, certain copper articles, and certain 
   166                  aluminum and steel derivative articles shall be set at 
   167                  an ad valorem rate of duty of 50 percent, with reduced 
   168                  rates available for certain products from the United 
   169                  Kingdom given the ongoing discussions and for 
   170                  derivative articles made entirely with metals 
   171                  originating from the United States. Full-value tariffs 
   172                  on certain copper articles and certain aluminum and 
   173                  steel derivative articles shall generally be set at an 
   174                  ad valorem rate of duty of 25 percent, with reduced 
   175                  rates available for certain derivative articles from 
   176                  the United Kingdom given the ongoing discussions 
   177                  between the United Kingdom and the United States and 
   178                  for derivative articles made entirely with metals 
   179                  originating from the United States.
   180  
   181                  10. I further determine that it is necessary and 
   182                  appropriate to terminate the aluminum, steel, and 
   183                  copper derivatives inclusions processes established in 
   184                  Proclamation 10895, Proclamation 10896, and 
   185                  Proclamation 10962. I authorize the Secretary and the 
   186                  United States Trade Representative (Trade 
   187                  Representative) to include additional derivative 
   188                  articles within the scope of the tariffs, on a rolling 
   189                  basis, when they jointly determine that imports of 
   190                  those derivative articles threaten to undermine the 
   191                  actions taken to address
   192  
   193  [[Page 18203]]
   194  
   195                  the national security risks identified in Proclamation 
   196                  9704, Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 10962. In 
   197                  determining whether to include additional derivative 
   198                  articles within the scope of the tariffs, the Secretary 
   199                  and the Trade Representative may solicit information, 
   200                  feedback, recommendations, or other relevant materials 
   201                  from domestic producers, industry associations, or 
   202                  other interested parties.
   203  
   204                  11. I also determine that it is necessary and 
   205                  appropriate to modify the scope of derivative articles 
   206                  subject to tariffs pursuant to Proclamation 9704, as 
   207                  amended, and Proclamation 9705, as amended. These 
   208                  determinations are based on new information and 
   209                  recommendations provided by the Secretary on whether a 
   210                  derivative article sufficiently contributes to the 
   211                  applicable national security threats found in 
   212                  Proclamation 9704 and Proclamation 9705, whether 
   213                  imposing tariffs on the derivative article is necessary 
   214                  to prevent circumvention of the tariffs on steel or 
   215                  aluminum articles, and whether a tariff on the full 
   216                  customs value of the derivative article will enable the 
   217                  tariff regimes, at this time, to address as effectively 
   218                  the national security threats found in Proclamation 
   219                  9704 and Proclamation 9705.

   222                  proclamation are necessary and appropriate to adjust 
   223                  imports of metal products to address more effectively 
   224                  the threats to the national security found in 
   225                  Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 
   226                  10962, including by, among other things, more 
   227                  effectively and quickly strengthening domestic 
   228                  manufacturing of metal products; reducing reliance on 
   229                  foreign manufacturing and importation of metal 
   230                  products; encouraging companies to expand domestic 
   231                  production capacity of metal products; increasing 
   232                  domestic research and development of metal products so 
   233                  that United States producers can produce cutting-edge 
   234                  technologies that are essential to the United States 
   235                  defense industrial base; and training workers to 
   236                  produce these strategic products.

   238                  13. Section 232 authorizes the President to adjust the 
   239                  imports of an article and its derivatives that are 
   240                  being imported into the United States in such 
   241                  quantities or under such circumstances as to threaten 
   242                  to impair the national security of the United States so 
   243                  that such imports will not threaten to impair the 
   244                  national security.

   247                  (19 U.S.C. 2483) (section 604), authorizes the 
   248                  President to embody in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule 
   249                  of the United States (HTSUS) the substance of statutes

   251                  including the removal, modification, continuance, or 
   252                  imposition of any rate of duty or other import 
   253                  restriction.
