    56                  Proclamation 11032 of June 1, 2026
    57  
    58                  
    59  Further Adjusting the Tariff Regimes for Imports 
    60                  of Aluminum, Steel, and Copper Into the United States
    61  
    62                  By the President of the United States of America
    63  
    64                  A Proclamation
    65  
    66                  1. In Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    67                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), as 
    68                  amended; Proclamation 9705 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    69                  Imports of Steel Into the United States), as amended; 
    70                  and Proclamation 10962 of July 30, 2025 (Adjusting 
    71                  Imports of Copper Into the United States), as amended, 
    72                  I found, under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act 
    73                  of 1962, as amended, 19 U.S.C. 1862 (section 232), that 
    74                  aluminum, steel, and copper are being imported into the 
    75                  United States in such quantities or under such 
    76                  circumstances as to threaten to impair the national 
    77                  security of the United States and took action under 
    78                  section 232 to adjust imports of aluminum, steel, and 
    79                  copper articles and their derivative articles 
    80                  (collectively, metal products) so that such imports 
    81                  will not threaten to impair the national security. 
    82                  Specifically, to address the national security threats 
    83                  found in Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9705, and 
    84                  Proclamation 10962, I established tariff regimes, which 
    85                  included imposing additional ad valorem duties on 
    86                  certain imports of metal products.
    87  
    88                  2. In Proclamation 11021 of April 2, 2026 
    89                  (Strengthening Actions Taken To Adjust Imports of 
    90                  Aluminum, Steel, and Copper Into the United States), I 
    91                  modified the tariff regimes established under section 
    92                  232 for imports of metal products to more effectively 
    93                  address the national security threats found in 
    94                  Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 
    95                  10962. In particular, I imposed an ad valorem duty of 
    96                  50 percent on products made of those metals; an ad 
    97                  valorem duty of 25 percent on derivative products that 
    98                  tend to be predominately composed of those metals; and 
    99                  a temporarily-reduced ad valorem duty of 15 percent on 
   100                  a subset of derivative products, namely fixed 
   101                  industrial machinery and power equipment.
   102  
   103                  3. Based on the Secretary of Commerce's (Secretary) 
   104                  monitoring and consultation with other senior 
   105                  officials, among other things, the Secretary has 
   106                  provided me information, opinions, and recommendations 
   107                  regarding the tariff regimes imposed in Proclamation 
   108                  9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as amended; and 
   109                  Proclamation 10962, as amended, and the national 
   110                  security threats found in those proclamations. Among 
   111                  other things, the Secretary has informed me that recent 
   112                  circumstances have affected and are affecting domestic 
   113                  industries that use agricultural equipment, industrial 
   114                  equipment and machinery, and other related products. 
   115                  Many products in these categories are treated as 
   116                  derivative articles of aluminum or steel because they 
   117                  tend to be predominantly composed of aluminum or steel. 
   118                  These products also serve an important role in 
   119                  productive domestic economic activity. For example, 
   120                  American farmers use agricultural equipment to produce 
   121                  the food upon which our Nation relies; construction 
   122                  equipment is essential for the continued 
   123                  reindustrialization of our Nation; and material-
   124                  handling equipment enables industrial logistics and 
   125                  factory operations.
   126  
   127                  4. To account for these circumstances, the Secretary 
   128                  recommended that I modify the tariffs imposed on these 
   129                  products pursuant to Proclamation 9704, as amended, and 
   130                  Proclamation 9705, as amended. In particular, the 
   131                  Secretary recommended that I expand the category of 
   132                  derivative products
   133  
   134  [[Page 34086]]
   135  
   136                  subject to the temporarily-reduced 15 percent ad 
   137                  valorem duty to include agricultural equipment and 
   138                  certain heating, ventilation, and air conditioning 
   139                  (HVAC) systems and components that are predominately 
   140                  for residential use, which are currently treated as 
   141                  aluminum or steel derivative products. The Secretary 
   142                  also recommended that I temporarily modify the tariffs 
   143                  imposed on mobile industrial equipment and machinery to 
   144                  support the American businesses and factories that use 
   145                  these products.
   146  
   147                  5. In addition, the Secretary has recommended that I 
   148                  include two types of aluminum and steel products 
   149                  (aluminum lithographic plates and steel racks) that are 
   150                  not currently subject to aluminum and steel tariffs 
   151                  within the product coverage of Proclamation 11021, to 
   152                  ensure that they are subject to the appropriate tariffs 
   153                  for aluminum and steel derivative products and to 
   154                  ensure that the purpose of the tariff regimes to 
   155                  address the national security threats found in 
   156                  Proclamation 9704 and Proclamation 9705 are not 
   157                  undermined. The Secretary also recommended that I 
   158                  modify the threshold for imported products to qualify 
   159                  as made ``entirely'' from American aluminum, steel, or 
   160                  copper, as that term is used in Proclamation 11021.
   161  
   162                  6. After considering the current information, opinions, 
   163                  and recommendations newly provided by the Secretary; 
   164                  the factors in section 232 (19 U.S.C. 1862(d)); the 
   165                  need to address the national security threats found in 
   166                  Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 
   167                  10962; and other relevant factors and information, I 
   168                  determine that it is necessary and appropriate to 
   169                  modify, as further described below, the tariff regimes 
   170                  for metal products imposed in Proclamation 9704, as 
   171                  amended, Proclamation 9705, as amended, and 
   172                  Proclamation 10962, as amended.
   173  
   174                  7. I determine that agricultural equipment and certain 
   175                  HVAC systems and components that are predominantly for 
   176                  residential use shall be included in the category of 
   177                  derivative products subject to the temporarily-reduced 
   178                  15 percent ad valorem duty under Proclamation 11021. In 
   179                  my judgment, this modification appropriately accounts 
   180                  for these products' roles in productive economic 
   181                  activity in the United States and accounts for recent 
   182                  circumstances affecting the relevant industries and 
   183                  services that use these products, while also enabling 
   184                  the tariff regimes to continue effectively addressing 
   185                  the national security threats found in Proclamation 
   186                  9704 and Proclamation 9705.
   187  
   188                  8. I determine that it is necessary and appropriate to 
   189                  temporarily modify the tariffs imposed on mobile 
   190                  industrial equipment and machinery, as detailed below. 
   191                  In my judgment, this temporary modification 
   192                  appropriately accounts for these products' roles in 
   193                  productive economic activity in the United States and 
   194                  accounts for recent circumstances affecting the 
   195                  relevant industries and services that use these 
   196                  products, while also allowing the tariff regimes to 
   197                  continue effectively addressing the national security 
   198                  threats found in Proclamation 9704 and Proclamation 
   199                  9705.
   200  
   201                  9. I determine that aluminum lithographic plates and 
   202                  steel racks constitute aluminum and steel derivative 
   203                  products that should be subject to the applicable 
   204                  derivative tariff under Proclamation 11021. In my 
   205                  judgment, subjecting these products to the derivative 
   206                  tariff in Proclamation 11021 will ensure that the 
   207                  tariffs on metal products are not circumvented and that 
   208                  the purpose of the actions to address the national 
   209                  security threats found in Proclamation 9704 and 
   210                  Proclamation 9705 is not undermined.
   211  
   212                  10. I determine that it is appropriate to modify the 
   213                  threshold for imported products to qualify as made 
   214                  ``entirely'' from American aluminum, steel, or copper, 
   215                  as that term is used in Proclamation 11021. The current 
   216                  threshold of 95 percent shall be modified to 85 
   217                  percent. In my judgment, this modification will 
   218                  incentivize increased use of American aluminum, steel, 
   219                  and copper in downstream derivative products and 
   220                  further the purpose of the actions to address the 
   221                  national security threats found in Proclamation 9704, 
   222                  Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 10962.
   223  
   224  [[Page 34087]]
   225  
   226                  11. Section 232 authorizes the President to adjust the 
   227                  imports of an article and its derivatives that are 
   228                  being imported into the United States in such 
   229                  quantities or under such circumstances as to threaten 
   230                  to impair the national security of the United States so 
   231                  that such imports will not threaten to impair the 
   232                  national security.
   233  
   234                  12. Section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended, 
   235                  19 U.S.C. 2483 (section 604), authorizes the President 
   236                  to embody in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the 
   237                  United States (HTSUS) the substance of statutes 
   238                  affecting import treatment, and actions thereunder, 
   239                  including the removal, modification, continuance, or 
   240                  imposition of any rate of duty or other import 
   241                  restriction.
   242  
   243                  NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the 
   244                  United States of America, by the authority vested in me 
   245                  by the Constitution and the laws of the United States, 
   246                  including section 232, section 604, and section 301 of 
   247                  title 3, United States Code, do hereby proclaim as 
   248                  follows:
   249  
   250                  (1) Effective with respect to goods entered for 
   251                  consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for 
   252                  consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight 
   253                  time on June 8, 2026, subchapter III of chapter 99 of 
   254                  the HTSUS is modified as provided in Annex IV to this 
   255                  proclamation and the lists of products provided in 
   256                  Annex I-A, Annex I-B, Annex II, and Annex III of 
   257                  Proclamation 11021 are modified as set forth in the 
   258                  annexes to this proclamation.
   259  
   260                  (2) Effective with respect to goods entered for 
   261                  consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for 
   262                  consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight 
   263                  time on June 8, 2026, until 11:59 p.m. eastern standard 
   264                  time on December 31, 2027, the applicable additional ad 
   265                  valorem rate of duty imposed pursuant to section 232 
   266                  under Proclamation 9704, as amended, and Proclamation 
   267                  9705, as amended, for all aluminum and steel articles 
   268                  listed in Annex I-C to this proclamation shall be:
   269  
   270                      (a) 25 percent, unless a lower rate of duty applies 
   271                  pursuant to clause (2)(b), (2)(c), or (2)(d) of this 
   272                  proclamation;
   273                      (b) For products of Argentina, Ecuador, El 
   274                  Salvador, Guatemala, Japan, the Republic of Korea, 
   275                  Liechtenstein, Switzerland, Taiwan, the United Kingdom, 
   276                  or a member nation of the European Union, the rate of 
   277                  duty shall be determined by the product's current ad 
   278                  valorem (or ad valorem equivalent) rate of duty under 
   279                  Column 1 of the HTSUS (Column 1 Duty Rate). For 
   280                  products of these jurisdictions with a Column 1 Duty 
   281                  Rate that is less than 15 percent, the sum of the 
   282                  Column 1 Duty Rate and the additional section 232 ad 
   283                  valorem rate of duty pursuant to this clause, shall be 
   284                  15 percent. For products of these jurisdictions with a 
   285                  Column 1 Duty Rate that is at least 15 percent, the 
   286                  additional section 232 ad valorem rate of duty imposed 
   287                  pursuant to this clause shall be zero percent;
   288                      (c) 10 percent, determined based on the product's 
   289                  current ad valorem (or ad valorem equivalent) Column 1 
   290                  Duty Rate in the same manner outlined in clause (2)(b) 
   291                  of this proclamation, for derivative articles the 
   292                  aluminum content of which is composed entirely of 
   293                  aluminum that was smelted and cast in the United 
   294                  States, or the steel content of which is composed 
   295                  entirely of steel that was melted and poured in the 
   296                  United States; and
   297                      (d) For products of Canada and Mexico that qualify 
   298                  for preferential tariff treatment under the United 
   299                  States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, a duty of 25 percent 
   300                  shall apply only to the non-U.S. content of the 
   301                  product. For purposes of this clause, ``non-U.S. 
   302                  content'' means the total value of the product minus 
   303                  the value attributable to parts produced in the United 
   304                  States. Notwithstanding the foregoing, the total 
   305                  effective duty on the imported product assessed under 
   306                  this subclause shall not be less than 15 percent ad 
   307                  valorem, as detailed in Annex IV of this proclamation. 
   308                  The Secretary shall issue guidance to U.S. Customs and 
   309                  Border Protection (CBP) regarding the assessment of 
   310                  ``U.S. content'' for purposes of this clause. If CBP 
   311                  determines that an importer has engaged in fraud or has 
   312                  deliberately misled the United States Government 
   313                  regarding the United States content of an imported 
   314                  product, CBP shall impose penalties to the extent 
   315                  permitted by law.
   316  
   317  [[Page 34088]]
   318  
   319                  (3)(a) Effective with respect to goods entered for 
   320                  consumption or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption

content.text:
Important Q13: machine listed Annex I-C, Canada qualifies USMCA, U.S. parts 60k, value 200k. Clause 2(d): Canada/Mexico USMCA duty 25% only on non-U.S. content, total effective not less than 15% ad valorem. Non-US content = 200-60=140k; 25%=35k; floor 15% of 200k =30k => 35k. So (a) $35,000.
(b) no US content: non-US 200k *25%=50k; floor 30k => 50k.
(c) Canada does not qualify USMCA, US parts 60k: clause 2(a) 25% of full customs value? Wait Annex I-C base rate 25% under 2(a), unless lower under b/c/d. Canada non-USMCA doesn't get 2(d); 25% of full value = 50k. Does U.S. content reduce? No. (c) 50k.
(d) Japan product, MFN 2.5%, Annex I-C. Clause 2(b): Japan is in list of jurisdictions, rate determined by Column1; MFN 2.5<15 => sum MFN + 232 =15%; section232 additional =12.5% of value =25k. Note clause 2(a) 25 unless lower; 2(b) yields 12.5% additional (total 15). So $25k.
(e) As (a), U.S. parts 20k, plus 30k attributable to aluminum smelted and cast in U.S. contained in a part made in Canada. Clause 2(d) non-U.S. content means total minus value attributable to parts produced in U.S. Does aluminum smelted/cast in U.S. contained in Canadian part count as U.S. content? Definition only "parts produced in the United States." The Q likely tests clause 4 85% threshold? Hmm. U.S. parts 20k, plus U.S. aluminum 30k in Canadian part. For 2(d), non-U.S. content = total minus value attributable to parts produced in U.S. = 180k; 25%=45k; floor 30k. But clause 2(c) 10% for derivative articles whose aluminum content is composed entirely of aluminum smelted and cast in U.S. Here machine is steel article? Q13 says steel article listed Annex I-C; most steel/aluminum melted outside U.S.; further30k aluminum smelted/cast U.S. contained in Canadian part. Does 2(c) apply if aluminum content entirely U.S.? No, most steel/aluminum outside U.S. Also machine is steel article, so aluminum content isn't the steel content. Clause 2(c) requires steel content entirely U.S., which it isn't. So 2(d) 25% non-U.S. content; but could U.S. aluminum content count toward "U.S. content" in Annex IV? Clause 2(d) definition says "value attributable to parts produced in the United States," not metals. The 30k is in a part made in Canada, so not a U.S.-produced part. Thus only 20k reduces. Duty 45k. But need consider "total effective duty not less than 15 percent" =30k; 45k > floor. So $45k.
(f) same as (e) but entered Oct6. Did anything change? The July 20 aluminum proclamation 11045 "Further Strengthening Actions Taken To Adjust Imports of Aluminum" maybe modifies Annex I-C or rates effective Aug1? Q13 asks Oct20 default, (f) Oct6. This suggests a change between Oct6 and Oct20! Need investigate 2026-14990 (July20) and maybe another. Search later docs affecting aluminum. The July20 proclamation may change USMCA content treatment effective Aug1? Let's read.

July20 aluminum only onshoring program, not machine. Q13(f) Oct6 vs Oct20 likely due to another proclamation? Wait Q13 says assume machine listed Annex I-C June. (f) same as (e), but entered Oct6. Why different date? Could be section 232 duty rate under Annex I-C expires/changes? No, June clause 2 applies until Dec31 2027. Maybe Oct6 is before something effective Oct? Search after July for steel/aluminum/mobile machinery. There may be "Adjusting Imports of Wind Turbines" or other but not machine. The difference may be that the machine is a steel article and October 6 vs October 20 crosses a change in IEEPA? No.

Wait Q13(h) "Until when does treatment in (a) apply, and what applies afterwards?" That refers June 2(d) Canada USMCA reduced duty, which applies until Dec31 2027, after which clause 3 rates of Proclamation 11021 (50%?) apply. So Q13(f) likely not about date change but tests a different aspect: maybe section 338 motor vehicle duty starts? But Q13 asks section 232 duty only. (f) Oct6 maybe before a section 232 change? Hmm.

Maybe there is an October 2026 proclamation that changes Annex I-C treatment effective Oct 15? Search "Annex I-C" across 2026 proclamations.

content.text:
Not relevant; effective likely 2027.

Back to Q13(f): maybe October 6 is before the October 20 "default" because Q wants test time-of-entry under a change effective October 15? Let's search all docs for "October 15" maybe no. Perhaps the change is not section232 but Section 338: On Oct6, the machine may be subject to section338 if listed in motor Annex II; but Q says "on no section 338 list." So no.

Could be simply to test that duty rate is determined by entry date, and October 6 is before October 20 but same rate. Maybe (f) is included to see if you incorrectly apply something effective October 20. What happens Oct20? The October scope proclamation applies Oct30, not Oct20. Maybe a section 301 amendment? No.

Wait Q13 default date Oct20 might be chosen because the June Annex I-C "temporary" treatment for mobile industrial machinery could have a 15% rate that expires 90 days after June 8? Let's read preamble "temporarily modify tariffs imposed on mobile industrial equipment and machinery" and clause 2. Clause 2 gives Annex I-C rates 25 until Dec31 2027. Not.

Maybe Annex IV contains a specific rate for mobile industrial machinery of 15% that applies only through a date, and Q13(f) tests it? But Annex IV is image not readable. Q13 assumptions: "machine is a steel article listed in Annex I-C ...". It asks section232 duty; perhaps Annex I-C itself includes a subcategory with rate 25; no need image. The scenario says product is listed; we need apply clause 2. (f) likely just an entry before default, perhaps to test section 338/301 not asked? We'll answer same as (e), noting no date-based change in the readable text.

But Q13(h): "Until when does the treatment in (a) apply, and what applies afterwards?" Clause 2 says until Dec31 2027, then clause 3 rates of 11021 (which for Annex I-A? For Annex I-C, 50%? Let's determine). Clause 3(a): effective Jan1 2028, rates for Annex I-C shall be rates set out in clause 3 of Proclamation 11021. Proclamation 11021 clause 3 is 25% for Annex I-B copper/derivative articles, not 50. Wait for Annex I-C products, clause 3 of 11021 maybe 25%. Yes, Proclamation 11021 had Annex I-A 50%, Annex I-B 25%, Annex III 15%. Annex I-C is a subset of derivative articles? Clause 3(a) says rates in clause 3 of 11021 = 25% generally. So after Dec31 2027, 25% full value? But if Canada USMCA maybe does 11021 clause 3 have Canada USMCA reduction? No, 2(d) is in 11032 and expires; so afterwards 25% full value (or 15% for UK etc). Need say clause 3 of 11021 (25% for Annex I-B/Annex I-C category). But wait 11021 clause 3 applies to "copper articles and aluminum and steel derivative articles listed in Annex I-B"; 11032 says for Annex I-C products, rates set out in clause 3 of 11021. So 25% unless lower for UK or all-US metal. For Canada USMCA, no content-based reduction after 2027. Good.

Q15 very hard. Let's map duties by entry date.

Products: aluminum extrusions of heading 7604, product of Canada, customs value 100k, all aluminum.
- Section 232 aluminum duty: 50% on full value from June4 2025 onward (except earlier 25% from Mar12 2025). Before Mar12 2025: 10% aluminum duty (from 2018), but question starts Feb10 2025. Need include 10% for Feb10. Q15 says "From April 6, 2026 the extrusions are entered under section 232 heading 9903.82.02." But for earlier entries, they were still aluminum articles under section232 at 25%/50%. We need rate as of each date.
- IEEPA northern border: 25% from Mar4 2025 to Jul31 2025; 35% from Aug1 2025 to Feb20 2026. USMCA exempt from Mar7 2025 onward. Non-USMCA pays. Did IEEPA apply to aluminum extrusions? Yes all Canadian products except energy. Did section232 stack? IEEPA orders had stacking rules; likely section232 and IEEPA stack? Need know EO 14289 stacking. For Q15, "every additional duty that the Federal Register imposed on these goods on the entry date counts." IEEPA duty likely applies in addition to 232. But EO 14289 may exclude IEEPA duties on 232 goods? Need check. This is crucial. Search EO 14289.

Crucial: Section 3(a)(ii): IEEPA northern/southern duties not stack with section 232 aluminum/steel; 232 prevails. Section 3(a)(iii): aluminum and steel 232 duties stack with each other. So for aluminum extrusions, from Mar4 2025 onward, IEEPA does NOT apply because 232 aluminum duty applies. Before May16? EO applies retroactively to Mar4 2025. Thus Feb10 2025: no IEEPA (not effective yet); 232 10%. Mar6 2025: 232 25%? Wait 232 increase effective Mar12, so on Mar6 aluminum 10%, IEEPA 25% effective Mar4. EO 14289 retroactively says IEEPA doesn't stack with 232, 232 10% applies. So Mar6: 10% 232 only. Mar10: same 10%. Mar14: IEEPA 25% but 232 25% from Mar12; 232 prevails, IEEPA 0. This seems likely why dates chosen! Great.
Jun3 2025: 232 25% (50% starts Jun4), IEEPA nonstacking => 25%.
Jun10 2025: 232 50%, IEEPA 0.
Aug5 2025: 232 50%, IEEPA 35% but no stack => 50%.
Mar2 2026: 232 50%, IEEPA ended Feb20 => 50%. Temporary surcharge? Effective Feb24 2026, 10%, but section232 articles exempt (Annex). So 50%.
Jun10 2026: 232 50%, surcharge expired Jul24; but does surcharge apply and exempt 232? yes not. 50%.
Jul27 2026: 232 50%; section301 Canada 10% effective Jul24, but 232 articles exempt under section301 note 52(f)(1) ("articles of aluminum... nor derivative aluminum... provided for headings 9903.82.02..."). Extrusions entered under 9903.82.02, exempt. So 50%.
Aug25 2026: 232 50%; section338 motor 50% from Aug22; but original clause 2 says 338 doesn't apply to articles subject to 232. Does later motor scope modification effective Sept15 change; Aug25 before Sept15, so 338 0. Section301 0. So 50%.
Sep14 2026: 232 50%; section338? Motor scope modification effective Sept15, so still original exemption on Sep14 => 0. Section301 0. So 50%.
Sep16 2026: 232 50%; motor scope modification effective Sept15 says 338 applies in addition to 232. Product listed Annex II since signed, on no Part A/B/exclusion. Thus 338 50% = 50k. Section301 0. Total 100k additional.
Nov10 2026: 232 50%, 338 50%, section301 0 = 100k.
Q15 asks "For each entry date below, give every duty owed in addition to MFN duty, by legal authority, with amount and total, and for each other additional duty then in force on products of Canada, say in a line why it is not owed. Do this for two cases: Case N no USMCA; Case U USMCA claim."

Need distinguish Case U for IEEPA: USMCA exempt from Mar7 2025; before Mar7, USMCA no exemption, so Mar6 case U still IEEPA? But nonstacking means 232 applies anyway. Feb10 no IEEPA. Mar6: IEEPA would apply but nonstacking 232. So same. Mar10: USMCA exempt IEEPA, 232. Same. For 232 no USMCA exemption (section 232 applies regardless). So all dates results same for N and U! Is that intended? Maybe section 232 has Canada USMCA exclusions? Aluminum 232 applies to all countries, no USMCA exemption since Mar12 2025. So Case N and U same. But question explicitly asks two cases likely expects differences for IEEPA on Mar6? Let's see:
- Feb10 2025: no IEEPA; 232 10% = 10k both.
- Mar6 2025: 232 pre-increase 10%; IEEPA 25% effective Mar4, USMCA exemption not until Mar7. Nonstacking EO 14289 retroactive to Mar4: IEEPA doesn't stack with 232; 232 10% only. Both same.
- Mar10: 232 10%, IEEPA 25% but nonstacking; USMCA exempt anyway. Both 10k.
- Mar14: 232 25%, IEEPA nonstack; both 25k.
So indeed same. Why two cases? Maybe because IEEPA USMCA exemption starts Mar7, but nonstacking makes it moot. Could be trick.

But wait Section 232 10% for Feb10 and Mar6/Mar10? Aluminum rate increased to 25% March12. Yes.

Check whether aluminum extrusions are "derivative aluminum articles" or "aluminum articles." Heading 7604 bars/rods/profiles are aluminum articles under Proclamation 9704 Annex. 10%/25%/50%.

Q15 also asks "for each other additional duty then in force on products of Canada, say in a line why it is not owed." Need list other duties in force by date:
- Feb10 2025: IEEPA northern border not yet effective (Feb4 paused to Mar4); no section301; no 338; no surcharge. Maybe section 232 only. 
- Mar6: IEEPA northern border effective but nonstacking with 232 under EO 14289; USMCA? not yet exempt but irrelevant.
- Mar10: same.
- Mar14: same; IEEPA doesn't stack.
- Jun3: IEEPA northern border 25% doesn't stack with 232; section232 25%.
- Jun10: 232 50%; IEEPA 25% doesn't stack; also IEEPA 35% later.
- Aug5: 232 50%; IEEPA 35% doesn't stack.
- Mar2 2026: 232 50%; IEEPA ended Feb20; temporary surcharge effective Feb24 but exempts section232 articles; section301 not yet; 338 not yet.
- Jun10 2026: 232 50%; surcharge 10% but exempts 232 articles; section301 not yet (July24); 338 not yet.
- Jul27 2026: 232 50%; surcharge? 150-day period ends Jul24, so expired; section301 10% but exempts 232 aluminum/derivative; 338 not yet.
- Aug25: 232 50%; section301 exempts; 338 original exemption for 232 until Sept15.
- Sep14: same.
- Sep16: 232 50%; 338 50% because motor scope modification effective Sept15 removed 232 exemption; section301 exempt; surcharge expired.
- Nov10: same as Sep16.

But what about IEEPA reciprocal tariffs (EO 14257) on Canada? Q15 says "every additional duty then in force on products of Canada." EO 14257 imposed 10% baseline reciprocal tariff (later perhaps 25%? Canada not listed in Annex I? Let's recall). EO 14257 April 2 2025 imposed 10% on all countries except those in Annex I? Canada maybe exempt? Need research. Also EO 14326 further modified reciprocal rates. Canada may have 25% reciprocal? But EO 14289 nonstacking sections 2(b)/2(c) only northern/southern border, not 14257 reciprocal. Section 3(a)(ii) doesn't cover reciprocal. IEEPA reciprocal tariffs might stack with 232? Need determine if Canada was subject to reciprocal tariff on aluminum extrusions. This could be significant. Let's research 14257 and amendments for Canada.

    73                  I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of 
    74                  America, find that underlying conditions, including a

    76                  relationships, disparate tariff rates and non-tariff 
    77                  barriers, and U.S. trading partners' economic policies 
    78                  that suppress domestic wages and consumption, as 
    79                  indicated by large and persistent annual U.S. goods 
    80                  trade deficits, constitute an unusual and extraordinary 
    81                  threat to the national security and economy of the 
    82                  United States. That threat has its source in whole or 
    83                  substantial part outside the United States in the 
    84                  domestic economic policies of key trading partners and 
    85                  structural imbalances in the global trading system. I 
    86                  hereby declare a national emergency with respect to 
    87                  this threat.
    88  
    89                  On January 20, 2025, I signed the America First Trade 
    90                  Policy Presidential Memorandum directing my 
    91                  Administration to investigate the causes of our 
    92                  country's large and persistent annual trade deficits in 
    93                  goods, including the economic and national security 
    94                  implications and risks resulting from such deficits, 
    95                  and to undertake a review of, and identify, any unfair 
    96                  trade practices by other countries. On February 13, 
    97                  2025, I signed a Presidential Memorandum entitled

    99                  review of our trading partners' non-reciprocal trading

   102                  2025, I received the final results of those 
   103                  investigations, and I am taking action today based on 
   104                  those results.
   105  
   106                  Large and persistent annual U.S. goods trade deficits 
   107                  have led to the hollowing out of our manufacturing 
   108                  base; inhibited our ability to scale advanced domestic 
   109                  manufacturing capacity; undermined critical supply 
   110                  chains; and rendered our defense-industrial base 
   111                  dependent on foreign adversaries. Large and persistent 
   112                  annual U.S. goods trade deficits are caused in 
   113                  substantial part by a lack of reciprocity in our 
   114                  bilateral trade relationships. This situation is 
   115                  evidenced by disparate tariff rates and non-tariff 
   116                  barriers that make it harder for U.S. manufacturers to 
   117                  sell their products in foreign markets. It is also 
   118                  evidenced by the economic policies of key U.S. trading 
   119                  partners insofar as they suppress domestic wages and 
   120                  consumption, and thereby demand for U.S. exports, while 
   121                  artificially increasing the competitiveness of their 
   122                  goods in global markets. These conditions have given 
   123                  rise to the national emergency that this order is 
   124                  intended to abate and resolve.
   125  
   126                  For decades starting in 1934, U.S. trade policy has 
   127                  been organized around the principle of reciprocity. The 
   128                  Congress directed the President to secure reduced 
   129                  reciprocal tariff rates from key trading partners first 
   130                  through bilateral trade agreements and later under the 
   131                  auspices of the global trading system. Between 1934 and 
   132                  1945, the executive branch negotiated and signed 32 
   133                  bilateral reciprocal trade agreements designed to lower 
   134                  tariff rates on a

   138                  reciprocal basis. After 1947 through 1994, 
   139                  participating countries engaged in eight rounds of 
   140                  negotiation, which resulted in the General Agreements 
   141                  on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) and seven subsequent tariff 
   142                  reduction rounds.

   144                  However, despite a commitment to the principle of 
   145                  reciprocity, the trading relationship between the 
   146                  United States and its trading partners has become 
   147                  highly unbalanced, particularly in recent years. The 
   148                  post-war international economic system was based upon 
   149                  three incorrect assumptions: first, that if the United 
   150                  States led the world in liberalizing tariff and non-
   151                  tariff barriers the rest of the world would follow; 
   152                  second, that such liberalization would ultimately 
   153                  result in more economic convergence and increased 
   154                  domestic consumption among U.S. trading partners 
   155                  converging towards the share in the United States; and 
   156                  third, that as a result, the United States would not 
   157                  accrue large and persistent goods trade deficits.
   158  
   159                  This framework set in motion events, agreements, and 
   160                  commitments that did not result in reciprocity or 
   161                  generally increase domestic consumption in foreign 
   162                  economies relative to domestic consumption in the 
   163                  United States. Those events, in turn, created large and

   168                  Members agreed to bind their tariff rates on a most-

   170                  best tariff rates to all WTO Members, they did not 
   171                  agree to bind their tariff rates at similarly low 
   172                  levels or to apply tariff rates on a reciprocal basis. 
   173                  Consequently, according to the WTO, the United States 
   174                  has among the lowest simple average MFN tariff rates in 
   175                  the world at 3.3 percent, while many of our key trading 
   176                  partners like Brazil (11.2 percent), China (7.5 
   177                  percent), the European Union (EU) (5 percent), India 
   178                  (17 percent), and Vietnam (9.4 percent) have simple 
   179                  average MFN tariff rates that are significantly higher.
   180  
   181                  Moreover, these average MFN tariff rates conceal much 
   182                  larger discrepancies across economies in tariff rates 
   183                  applied to particular products. For example, the United 
   184                  States imposes a 2.5 percent tariff on passenger

content.text:
Reciprocal 10% does not apply in addition to existing Canada border orders; and if those terminated, USMCA 0, non-USMCA 12%. So while IEEPA northern border active, reciprocal 10% not stack. But EO 14289 section 3? 14257 says 10% doesn't apply in addition to border orders. For aluminum 232, border order nonstacked, so reciprocal also likely 0. After border order terminated Feb20 2026, reciprocal 12%? Wait EO 14257 itself was terminated by EO 14389 (section 1 includes 14257). EO 14389 ended all IEEPA duties including reciprocal. So after Feb20 2026, none.

But what about during Mar-Jun 2025, reciprocal 10% on Canada? Section 2(d)-(e) says all Canada goods not USMCA already subject 25%; and any rate under this order shall not apply in addition. So 0. Good.

What about "temporary import surcharge" 10% Feb24-Jul24 2026: Section 122 excludes section232 articles (Annex I/II). So 0.

What about section 301 forced labor 10% from July24: note 52(f)(1) exempts aluminum/steel articles and derivative headings including 9903.82.02. So 0.

What about section 338: original motor Annex II product? Q15 says listed Annex II motor, on no Part A/B/exclusion. From Aug22 50%. Original clause 2 exempts section232 articles. But motor scope modification Sept15 says apply in addition to 232. On Aug25/Sep14, before Sept15, 338 0. On Sep16 onward, 338 50%. Good.

But wait on Sep16, is the product still in motor Annex II? Q15 assumptions: listed since signed and on no Part A, Part B or exclusion list. The Sept scope modification Part A adds products; Part B removes. Not on either means remains listed. Yes.

Also Q15 dates Mar6 and Mar10: IEEPA effective Mar4; but section232 aluminum rate 10% until Mar12. EO 14289 was signed Apr29 but applies retroactively to Mar4. So for a Mar6 entry, at time of entry IEEPA 25% may have been collected; but as Federal Register stands today, retroactive nonstacking means 232 only. Question says "duties legally owed ... as Federal Register stands today." So 10% only, with refund of IEEPA? We can note EO 14289 retroactive provides refunds.

Wait Section 232 10% from 2018 applied to Canada until March 12 2025? Yes, Canada was subject to 10% aluminum tariff from 2018? Actually Canada was exempt from 2018 aluminum tariffs after May 2019, then reimposed 10% in Aug 2020? Let's recall: Proclamation 9704 imposed 10% on most countries; Canada initially exempt? Canada was subject to 10% from June 1 2018, then exempt May 20 2019, then reimposed Aug 16 2020 (Proc 10060), then maybe removed? In Feb 2025 Proc 10895 says "terminate agreements with Canada... as of March 12, 2025; all imports from Canada subject to revised 25%". That suggests pre-March 12 Canada may have been exempt under alternative agreement! Uh oh. Q15 Feb10 2025 and Mar6/Mar10: Was Canada subject to 10% aluminum tariff? Need check. Proclamation 10895 recital 4: "In subsequent proclamations, the President adjusted tariffs applicable to aluminum from Argentina, Australia, Canada, Mexico, EU, UK after alternative ways..." Recital 7 says volume from countries excluded or alternative arrangements. Clause 4 says agreements with Canada etc ineffective as of Mar12, all imports subject to 25%. So before Mar12, Canada may have been exempt (0%) or under alternative arrangement, not 10%. Critical.

Let's inspect clause 4 more: It says Proclamation 10327 and 10690 with respect to EU; Proclamation 10405 UK ineffective. What about Canada? Search clauses for Canada.

content.text:
Yes, Canada exempt from aluminum tariffs before Mar12 2025 via Proc 9893/10106. So Feb10, Mar6, Mar10 aluminum duty = 0, not 10%. Then what duties apply? IEEPA northern border:
- Feb10: paused until Mar4, so no IEEPA. Section232 0. Other? No. So total additional $0.
- Mar6: IEEPA 25% effective Mar4. Canada not USMCA exempt until Mar7. Section232 0 (exempt until Mar12). So IEEPA 25% applies! EO 14289 nonstacking only if 232 applies; 232 0, so IEEPA 25k.
- Mar10: IEEPA 25%; USMCA exempt from Mar7, so Case U 0; Case N 25k. Section232 0.
- Mar14: IEEPA 25%; but Section232 25% now applies; EO 14289 nonstacking: IEEPA doesn't apply, so 232 25k both.
This explains two cases! Great.

Feb10 Case N/U 0.
Mar6 both 25k (USMCA exemption not yet).
Mar10 Case N 25k, Case U 0.
Mar14 both 25k (232, IEEPA nonstack).
Jun3: 232 25k (Canada now subject), IEEPA 25% nonstack => 25k.
Jun10: 232 50k, IEEPA 25% nonstack => 50k.
Aug5: 232 50k, IEEPA 35% nonstack => 50k.
Mar2 2026: IEEPA ended; 232 50k; surcharge 10% exempts 232 => 50k.
Jun10 2026: 232 50k; surcharge 10% exempts 232 => 50k.
Jul27: 232 50k; surcharge expired (Jul24); section301 exempt; 338 not yet => 50k.
Aug25: 232 50k; 338 original 232 exemption => 0; 301 exempt => 50k.
Sep14: 232 50k; 338 still exemption until Sep15 => 50k.
Sep16: 232 50k + 338 50k = 100k.
Nov10: same 100k.

But need revisit Feb10: Was IEEPA northern border originally effective Feb4 then paused to Mar4. Yes. So 0. Was there any other 10% aluminum tariff under section232? No. Good.

What about Feb10 2025 "temporary import surcharge" no. Reciprocal no. Section301 no. 338 no.

Mar6: Could Section232 derivative aluminum still apply at 10% even though Canada exempt from aluminum articles? Canada exemption Proc 9893/10106 may apply to aluminum articles only, not derivative articles? Clause 4 of 10895 says provisions of clause 1 of Proc 9980 as applicable to derivative aluminum from Argentina, Australia, Canada, Mexico ineffective Mar12; before that Canada exempt from derivative too. So 0. IEEPA 25%. Good.

Mar10 Case U: USMCA goods exempt from IEEPA effective Mar7. Case N pays 25%. Good.

Now Q15 "for each other additional duty then in force on products of Canada, say in a line why it is not owed." Need include reciprocal IEEPA 10%/12%, northern border, surcharge, 301, 338. We can summarize per date rather than exhaustive each duty each date, but requirement says for each other additional duty then in force. We can write a table with columns: 232, IEEPA border, reciprocal, surcharge, 301, 338, total. Then notes. That is efficient.

Need know whether reciprocal IEEPA 10% applied to Canada during Apr 2025-Feb 2026. EO 14257 section 2(d)-(e): all Canada goods already subject to border duties; reciprocal rate shall not apply in addition. For USMCA goods, border duty 0 but reciprocal? Section 2(e) says if border orders terminated, USMCA 0, non-USMCA 12%. While active, "Any ad valorem rate of duty ... under this order shall not apply in addition to the ad valorem rate of duty specified by existing orders." Could still apply 10% to USMCA goods because border rate 0? Need parse: 2(d) says all goods of Canada that do not qualify USMCA are presently subject to 25%; USMCA continue eligible. 2(e) says any rate under this order shall not apply in addition to the ad valorem rate specified by existing orders. This might mean reciprocal 10% doesn't stack on border 25%, but could apply to USMCA goods? However 2(e) second sentence: if border orders terminated, USMCA 0, non-USMCA 12%. This suggests during border orders, reciprocal order imposes no additional Canada duty at all (because Canada handled under border orders), including USMCA (0). So reciprocal 0 for all Canada until border orders ended. After Feb20, reciprocal order itself terminated. Good.

Need section 301 final effective July24, but Canada 10% and 232 exemption. For aluminum extrusions under 9903.82.02, note 52(f)(1) exempt. Good.

Need section 338 original effective Aug22; product is on Annex II motor. Before Sept15, 338 clause2 says no apply to 232. Good.

Need Q15 Case U for section 338: no USMCA exemption in section338. It doesn't matter.

Now Q14 #7 "no product will bear more than 12.5 percent duty in total." Note 52(a) says additional duties also subject to general rates; and 232 articles exempt from 301 but may bear 232 + 338; total can exceed. Incorrect.

Q11 discrepancies. Need systematically identify inaccuracies:
1. Dairy exclusion 11062 clause 3 refers to "Proclamation of September 8, 2026 (Modifying the Scope ... Dairy)" but no such proclamation exists. Cite 91 FR 58320 and search absence? We can say no such document in Federal Register; the only Sept8 dairy document is 11062 itself. This is a discrepancy between 11062 and the public record. Strong.
2. Alcohol exclusion 11061 recital 1 says duties effective August 19, but recital 4 and operative history say Aug22; 11056 changed to Aug22. Same in dairy 11062, motor exclusion 11063, alcohol scope 11064, motor scope 11065, Oct scope 11076 recital 1 says Aug19 while recital 4 says Aug22. Is that a "discrepancy"? Yes internal inconsistency. But Q11 asks one document's statement about what action provides vs operative text of that document or another. The recital statement "effective August 19" conflicts with operative clause 1 of 11056 (Aug22) and later recital. List once per document? "List each discrepancy once." Could group all six with same pattern, or list each. Better list as one recurring discrepancy across six documents with cites.
3. Alcohol/motor scope proclamations recital 1 says duties effective Aug19; operative clause 1 effective Sept15 for changes, and recital 4 says Aug22. Same pattern.
4. Suspension 11056 clause 1 says "chapeau of Annex II ... amended by deleting effective date 'August 19' and inserting 'August 22'" but the operative clauses 1 and 3 of Proclamations 11046/47/48 still say Aug19. It doesn't amend them. This is a textual inconsistency: clause 1 sets effective date Aug22 but only amends annex chapeau; the body remains Aug19. Q2(b). List as discrepancy.
5. Alcohol scope 11064 clause 1 says duties "shall apply in addition to duties imposed pursuant to section 232," while Proclamation 11046 clause 2 says duties "shall not apply to articles subject to duties pursuant to section 232." This is a change/amendment, but is it discrepancy? The scope proclamation does not expressly amend clause 2; it just states a contrary rule. Could list as conflict. Same motor 11065 vs 11048 clause 2. But maybe scope is later operative text and prevails; still a discrepancy between documents. Q11 likely expects.
6. Motor exclusion 11063 recital 1 says original effective Aug19; same.
7. October scope 11076 recital 5 says 11065 "modified the duties imposed under Proclamation 11048" — accurate.
8. Q11 in section 301: Final notice preamble line 170-174 says proposals "included exemptions for ... all articles and parts subject to section 232" but operative note 52(f) only exempts enumerated headings and says other 232 articles may be subject. Is this a discrepancy? The preamble is describing proposal, not adopted text. It says "The tariff proposals ... included exemptions..." That's true of proposal. But could be read as the action includes. Q11 asks "a statement in one document about what the action provides, or about what another document says or does" differs from operative text. Maybe final notice's SUMMARY says "imposing tariffs on all products ... with certain exemptions as provided in Annexes I and II" okay.
9. June proposal SUMMARY says "additional duties on all products ... except Annex A" and notes raw materials etc. The 10% list in June included "Canada, Ecuador, EU, Indonesia, Mexico, Pakistan" because they impose forced labor import prohibition, plus Argentina etc. Final notice says "The June 5 FRN proposed applying tariffs of 10 percent for each economy that imposes a forced labor import prohibition..." correct.
10. Final notice at lines 289-295 says exemptions include certain products of Argentina... list includes "Switzerland" etc. Fine.
11. Final notice line 1540 says "exempt all products proposed for exemption in Annex A except non-pharmaceutical applications of certain chemical products." Then line 1543 "not to remove additional products" — okay.
12. Q14 #2 itself not a discrepancy in docs.
13. June proposal line 266 "all of the investigated economies have failed both to impose a forced labor import prohibition and to effectively enforce such a prohibition" but earlier divides 54 failed to impose and enforce, 6 failed to effectively enforce. The sentence says all 60 failed both, which contradicts the categorization (for six, they imposed but failed to enforce; for 54, failed both). Actually line 266-268: "Therefore, all of the investigated economies have failed both to impose a forced labor import prohibition and to effectively enforce such a prohibition." This is internally inconsistent: six economies "have failed to effectively enforce a prohibition" implies they imposed it. This may be a discrepancy. Final notice lines 151-154 repeats same: "All ... have failed to impose ... and to effectively enforce..." while lines 147-150 say six failed to effectively enforce. Strong Q11 item.
14. Q14 #3: final notice says additional economies imposed bans: Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago; but the memo says same six, and final specific determinations for Cambodia/Guatemala/Honduras mention ART commitment and adoption; they were already 10% in proposal. No discrepancy there, just alert misreads.
15. Q14 #6: "471 more products than proposed" final says additional 471 products in each investigation. Fine.
16. Q14 #7: "no product >12.5 total" not in docs; not discrepancy.
17. Q11 maybe USTR final notice says "The June 5 FRN proposed ... all articles subject to section 232" (true), while adopted note 52(f) doesn't exempt all 232, only listed. Preamble later line 2031 says "many inputs, including auto parts already subject to Section 232 tariffs, are exempt from additional tariffs pursuant to this action." But note 52(f) lists only specific vehicle headings; if a 232 auto part heading not listed, not exempt. Maybe.
18. Q11: Final notice line 489-495 FTZ rule applies to "Any product ... subject to additional duty ... admitted into a U.S. foreign trade zone ... only may be admitted as privileged foreign status, except domestic status, effective as of date duty imposed." Memo/notice preamble Q14 #8. Good.
19. Q11: June notice line 307 says proposed exemptions include "all articles and parts currently subject to section 232 tariffs"; final notice line 171-173 says proposal included "all articles and parts ... subject to tariffs under Section 232." consistent.
20. Q11: Final notice line 1542 "Other than the products with non-pharmaceutical applications, as discussed below, the Trade Representative determined not to remove additional products from the exemption list." But then line 1590 section discusses requests to remove beef, avocados etc and says not remove. Consistent.
21. Q11: Final notice line 1648 "additional 471 products" vs line 1666 lists categories. Q14 #6 "including all sugar" contradicted by "certain sugar."
22. Q11: Suspension proclamation 11056 recital 4 says "suspending for a period of 3 days the additional duties" but clause 1 actually changes effective date, not suspends already-effective duties. Since signed Aug18 before Aug19 effective, it postpones start, not suspends. Later docs call it "temporarily suspended for 3 days the effective date." This is a statement vs operative mechanism. Maybe a discrepancy.
23. Q11: 11056 clause 1 says effective date Aug22, "Accordingly" amend chapeau Annex II. But the chapeau may not contain the effective date? The annex images not readable. We can note it amends only chapeau, not operative clauses.
24. Q11: September exclusion 11061 recital 6 says Canada maintained/increased discrimination "after additional duties became effective"; but recital 3 says Canada reneged Aug21 before duties became effective Aug22. It says "after issuance ... and after duties became effective" but the Saskatchewan announcement Aug27 is after. Fine.
25. Q11: Alcohol exclusion 11061 recital 2 says suspension "temporarily suspended for 3 days the effective date" — operative changed date by 3 days. Fine.
26. Q11: Q14 #1 memo deadline: memo says TRQs feasible by Sept1 but section 2 says "as soon as determines feasible"; not a discrepancy, but statement overreads.
27. Q11: Q14 #2 June notice 450 comments/nearly 60 witnesses vs final 1600/100. This is not a discrepancy; different proceedings. But Q14 asks evaluate.
28. Q11: Q14 #3: final notice says six economies adopted bans + Jordan ART, but the memo says "As a result of these actions ... goods of these economies should be tariffed at 10 percent" including Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras which already had ART commitments and were already proposed 10. Not discrepancy.
29. Q11: Q14 #4 "removed beef and avocados" contradicted final notice says not removed.
30. Q11: Q14 #5 "every net MFN has own list" contradicted specific determinations for Japan/Korea only Part A. But is this a law firm alert statement, not a document? Q14 asks evaluate statements, not Q11. Q11 only discrepancies in documents, not client alert.
31. Q11: Q14 #9 "if court holds exemption invalid, goods become subject" memo says yes; final notice section IV likely. Need read final section IV to see maybe differs.

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

(e) arrives Oct2: Annex exclusion effective Sept29, so excluded from importation; no entry/duty. But if "arrives" and is imported Oct2, import ban applies. No section338 or 301 because cannot import. If somehow entered, clause 2? It was not imported before Sept29, so ban. Answer: prohibited, no duty calculable. Need note if it had been imported before Sept29 but not entered, clause2 would preserve 50% 338, but facts say arrives Oct2.

Q3 similarly:
A arrives Sep10, entered Sep14: before exclusion effective; 338 50% of 30k =15k. Section301? Q3 asks section338 only. No.
B arrives Sep27, warehouse, withdrawn Oct5: imported before Sept29 but not entered before; clause2 says remain 50% duty. So may import? It was imported before ban; entry for consumption after effective? Clause2 says remain subject to 50% duty, so allowed with duty 15k.

D arrives 12:30am Sep29, entry that morning: imported on/after effective => excluded, cannot import, no duty.
A nuance: A arrives Sep10 and entered Sep14, before Sept29, so 338 duty. Yes.

(b) E arrives Sep25, admitted FTZ that day, entry for consumption Oct6. The import ban effective "goods imported on or after Sept29." Admission to FTZ is not importation into customs territory; entry for consumption Oct6 is importation. Thus ban applies; cannot enter. But original proclamation clause 4 requires privileged foreign status if admitted on/after effective date (Aug22) and subject to duty. If admitted Sep25, it must be privileged foreign status. Upon entry Oct6, ban prevents entry. If a court invalidates ban, 50% duty under 9(b). Need also mention if CBP treats FTZ admission as importation? The text says "imported"; under FTZ, goods not entered. Most defensible: ban applies at withdrawal because that is when entered/imported for consumption. But clause 2 says products imported but not yet entered before Sept29 remain 50%; E was admitted FTZ, not "imported" perhaps. We need flag uncertainty. Question asks "What duty or restriction applies?" Answer: import ban/restriction, no duty; because entry for consumption Oct6 is after effective date. If CBP considered it imported on Sept25, then it would be grandfathered 50% under clause2. We'll state primary reading and uncertainty.

(c) court invalidates ban as applied: clause 9(b) says 50% duty applies to the import to which invalidated ban applied before invalidation. Clause says "shall apply to the import to which the invalidated ... ban had applied before its invalidation." Could be interpreted the specific imports, not future. But severability provision intended fallback. Question asks "What applies to shipments of it imported after that ruling, and under which provision?" Answer: 50% section338 duty under 11061 clause 9(b) (and 11046), assuming product otherwise within Annex II and not excluded by scope modification. Q2.answer:
(a) **Entry 1 (Aug. 20, 2:00 p.m.): $0.** **Entry 2 (Aug. 21, 11:59 p.m.): $0.** **Entry 3 (Aug. 22, 12:01 a.m.): $20,000.** Entry 3 is exactly at the amended start time: $40,000 × 50% = $20,000. The controlling text is Proclamation 11046 clause (1), as moved by Proclamation 11056 clause (1): duty applies to goods entered for consumption or withdrawn for warehouse consumption on or after 12:01 a.m. ET Aug. 22, 2026.

(b) Proclamation 11046 clauses (1) and (3) each print “August 19, 2026,” and the Annex II chapeau also printed August 19. Proclamation 11056 clause (1) says the effective date “shall be” Aug. 22, 2026, and “Accordingly” amends **only the chapeau of Annex II** of each of 11046, 11047 and 11048 by deleting “August 19, 2026” and inserting “August 22, 2026.” It did **not** amend the operative clauses (1) and (3), which still read August 19. The later operative clause (1) of 11056 controls and fixes Aug. 22; the September proclamations (11061, 11064) confirm that the suspension lapsed and the duties became effective at 12:01 a.m. Aug. 22.

(c) The documents say a refund is available through CBP’s normal procedures. Proclamation 11056 clause (2) directs agencies to suspend collection as required, and clause (4) states that if implementation requires a refund, “refunds shall be processed pursuant to applicable law and CBP’s standard procedures for such refunds.” Entry 1 was before the operative start time, so the 50% deposit was not owed.

(d) No further presidential action was required for the duties to begin. Section 338’s 30-day waiting period ran from the July 20 findings; 11056 moved the start to Aug. 22. Later documents state that Canada “reneged” on Aug. 21, the three-day suspension “lapsed” at 12:01 a.m. Aug. 22, and the duties “became effective” then.

(e) The original start date was the earliest date permitted by section 338. The proclamations were signed July 20, 2026. Section 338 forbids the duty to take effect earlier than 30 days after the proclamation. Counting July 21 as day 1: July 21–31 = 11 days; Aug. 1–19 = 19 days; total 30 days. Hence Aug. 19, 2026, at 12:01 a.m. was the first permissible moment.
Q2.basis: Proclamation 11046 cl. (1) and (3), 91 FR 46641; Proclamation 11056 cl. (1), (2), (4), 91 FR 54790–91; Proclamation 11061 recitals 3–4, 91 FR 58311–12; Proclamation 11064 recitals 3–4, 91 FR 58331–32. Section 338 waiting period is recited in 11046 ¶10, 91 FR 46640–41.
Q2.uncertainty: The internal text conflict is real: 11046 clauses (1) and (3) were not conformed to Aug. 22. The later operative clause (1) of 11056 is the best reading; a broker should be prepared to cite it and the September confirmations.

Q3.answer:
(a) **A. $15,000 section 338 duty.** Arrives Sept. 10 and entered Sept. 14, before the Sept. 29 exclusion; $30,000 × 50% = $15,000. **B. $15,000.** Although it arrived Sept. 27, it was imported before Sept. 29 but not entered/withdrawn until Oct. 5; Proclamation 11061 clause (2) expressly keeps such goods at the 50% rate. $30,000 × 50% = $15,000. **C. $15,000.** Arrives 11:30 p.m. Sept. 28 but is not entered until 9:00 a.m. Sept. 29; imported before Sept. 29 but not entered before that time, so clause (2) keeps 50%. **D. Cannot be imported; no duty is owed because entry is prohibited.** Arrives 12:30 a.m. Sept. 29, on/after the effective time, so the import ban applies.

(b) **$15,000 section 338 duty; not the import ban.** It arrived Sept. 25, before the Sept. 29 effective time, but was not entered for consumption until Oct. 6. Proclamation 11061 clause (2) covers products “imported, but not yet entered for consumption” before Sept. 29 and keeps them at 50%. It also had to be admitted to the FTZ in privileged foreign status under Proclamation 11046 clause (4) because it was admitted after the duty’s effective date.

(c) The 50% section 338 duty applies to the import covered by the invalidated ban. Proclamation 11061 clause 9(b) says that if the import ban is invalidated in whole or in part as to any import, “the 50 percent ad valorem duty imposed in Proclamation 11046 shall apply to the import to which the invalidated import ban ... had applied before its invalidation.” For later shipments, the most defensible reading is that the same fallback 50% duty applies, because the exclusion is the only thing that displaced it; the clause is not expressly written as a prospective rate for future entries, however.

(d) No. Proclamation 11061 clause (3) says that, apart from changing the Annex products from duty to import ban, it “does not otherwise affect” the products that remain subject to the 50% duty. Listed Canadian alcoholic products not in the Annex remain at 50%.
Q3.basis: Proclamation 11061 cl. (1)–(3), (9)(b), 91 FR 58312–13; Proclamation 11046 cl. (1), (4), 91 FR 46641. The beer is assumed to be in Annex II of 11046, untouched by 11064, and in the Annex to 11061.
Q3.uncertainty: The FTZ point depends on reading “imported, but not yet entered for consumption” in 11061 clause (2) to cover FTZ admission; that is the natural reading of the clause, but the text does not separately mention FTZs. Clause 9(b) is also not explicit about future shipments after a court ruling.

(b) Proclamation 11076 was **signed Oct. 23, 2026**, **filed with the Office of the Federal Register Oct. 29, 2026**, and **published Oct. 30, 2026** (91 FR 68861). It applies to goods entered for consumption or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption on or after **12:01 a.m. ET Oct. 30, 2026**. The scope proclamations do not reach entries made before their effective times: each says the changes are effective “with respect to goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, on or after” the stated time. (c) Differences from the June proposal:
